Heb gymorth, gall y person ifanc yma gario craith gyflog rhwng 10 y cant a 15 y cant, sydd yn dal i'w gweld pan yn 42 oed, yn ddyfnach fyth ar ôl pob cyfnod pellach mas o waith. O ran dim ond yr allbwn economaidd, mae eithrio un person ifanc yn costio tua £100,000 gydol oes i'r gymdeithas gyfan. Yng Nghymru, fel rŷn ni wedi ei glywed, rŷn ni'n amcangyfrif bod tua 50,000 o bobl ifanc rhwng 16 a 24 oed sydd ddim mewn addysg, cyflogaeth na hyfforddiant. Mae hynny'n fethiant cymdeithasol ac yn un economaidd: 50,000 dyfodol yn culhau, a Chymru gyfan yn ysgwyddo'r gost.

Dylem fod yn fanwl gywir pwy ydyn nhw, gan fod y diagnosis yn penderfynu beth yw'r driniaeth. Dydyn nhw ddim yn un grŵp. Mae tua thraean yn ddi-waith yn yr ystyr gonfensiynol, yn chwilio am waith ond yn methu â dod o hyd iddo. Mae tua dwy ran o dair yn economaidd anweithgar, ddim yn chwilio am waith neu ddim yn gallu ei wneud, ac yma mae afiechyd, yn anad dim afiechyd meddwl, wedi dod yn un o'r gyrwyr sy'n tyfu gyflymaf. Y rhai a adawodd addysg gynharaf yw'r rhai mwyaf tebygol o aros ar wahân i’r farchnad lafur hiraf. Bydd system a adeiladwyd ar gyfer y rhai sydd yn ceisio gwaith yn unig yn parhau i golli'r grŵp mwy. Bydd system wedi'i hadeiladu o amgylch rhwystrau iechyd yn unig yn colli'r gweddill. Ac oherwydd bod y ffordd yn agor neu yn cau cyn i berson ifanc gyrraedd y farchnad lafur, mae ysgolion a cholegau yn rhan o'r ateb hefyd. Felly, mae angen ateb cyfansawdd sydd yn mynd i'r afael â'r holl ffactorau yma.

contributions.text_english:
It is right that, at the beginning of this new administration and this new Senedd, we ask some hard questions of the system we've inherited. This Government took office with spending on employability support marginally higher per head than other parts of the UK, and with the proportion of young people who are NEET rising sharply on the most recent survey data. So, higher spending in Wales, yet more young people currently adrift. I don't think anybody in the Siambr would find that acceptable, and the Government doesn't either.

One of the key questions for me is how long after disengaging does the system first reach a young person. Actually, is it the system that's disengaged from them, rather than the young people from the system? I've asked my officials to establish that number precisely. In designing any policy, of course investment matters, but as the Member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf said, outcomes matter more. The measure of success is not the number of job starts or the people on a programme that we can count, but whether a young person is still in good work or learning six months on, and 12 months on. And that's the standard I want applied to every programme in my portfolio.

The young person's guarantee was designed by the previous administration. Governments change but the commitment to young people should not and does not. Under this Government, under this Minister, I want it to grow even stronger. That's why we're proud to support the motion today. No young person in Wales should be left without a route into education, training or work. Our task is not to do less for young people, it's to do better by them, and doing better also demands honesty. Existing policies—UK and Welsh alike—under Governments of every colour have not been sufficient to the task. We need better.

We're not starting from a blank sheet of paper. Some of the most promising results internationally come from approaches that join up employment and health support together, and from guarantees that put a firm time limit on how long a young person waits for an offer. When I meet with Alan Milburn soon, I will discuss these ideas and how we can work as two Governments together. I want to work as a Minister with everyone in this Chamber, and with the cross-party group on youth employment—there's no monopoly on good ideas—and I want our work to be evidence led. I have to say that I haven't seen any convincing evidence myself that immigration is a major contributory factor for youth unemployment.

We do know some things about what works, and we can draw upon the experience of the New Deal for the unemployed, 25 years ago—one of the most successful interventions ever in terms of active labour market policy. We know that tens of thousands of young people are outside work and learning now, while Welsh employers still report vacancies they struggle to fill. What that tells me is that this isn't only about job preparation; it's structural.

It's no good if a job exists but you never hear about it, or you haven't heard about the young person's guarantee, or you can't afford the bus to reach it, or the bus route doesn't even exist to help you get there. Support on its own is not enough because you cannot train a young person into a job that does not exist. So, you need work on the demand side as well as on the supply side. The work of our new development agency in helping to scale Welsh firms, in building the sectors of the future, and in helping some of our traditional sectors like tourism and food and drink to provide those first jobs, is critical. And we will be asking more of employers. To echo the point that was made by one of the Members here, Governments can do so much, but Governments on their own cannot do everything, and in creating first jobs, we need employers to do more as well.

There's a harder challenge that has been on the horizon and has now arrived. Artificial intelligence, on the early evidence, is not abolishing occupations, but it is stripping out the routine tasks from which entry levels were traditionally built in administration, in customer service, in junior professional work. If firms do not redesign the first rung, it will simply disappear. Our responsibility as a Government is to help make sure that technological change expands opportunity rather than narrows it, and we need the skills system to enable us to do that. Our support right across Government must answer the labour market of tomorrow, not the one of 10 or 15 years ago.

None of this works if a young person cannot find the way in. Too often, we ask the young people that are furthest away from the labour market to navigate the most fragmented part of our public services. Trusted relationships help a young person back into the system: youth services, councils, employers, colleges, trade unions, community organisations. Our job is to make those connections simpler and stronger so that no young person has to tell their story twice.

Llywydd, fair work gives more than a wage; it gives purpose, routine, a place amongst others, community. We'll keep testing what works. We'll ground that in the evidence and the lived experience of young people. We'll be honest about what does not. We'll change course where the evidence demands it. Our focus will be relentlessly on outcomes, not just activity, and the test of everything is simple: whether we reach that 19-year-old in Rhyl sooner, offer them something worth taking, and build a first rung that holds. Diolch.

The young person's guarantee was designed by the previous administration. Governments change but the commitment to young people should not and does not. Under this Government, under this Minister, I want it to grow even stronger. That's why we're proud to support the motion today. No young person in Wales should be left without a route into education, training or work. Our task is not to do less for young people, it's to do better by them, and doing better also demands honesty. Existing policies—UK and Welsh alike—under Governments of every colour have not been sufficient to the task. We need better.

We're not starting from a blank sheet of paper. Some of the most promising results internationally come from approaches that join up employment and health support together, and from guarantees that put a firm time limit on how long a young person waits for an offer. When I meet with Alan Milburn soon, I will discuss these ideas and how we can work as two Governments together. I want to work as a Minister with everyone in this Chamber, and with the cross-party group on youth employment—there's no monopoly on good ideas—and I want our work to be evidence led. I have to say that I haven't seen any convincing evidence myself that immigration is a major contributory factor for youth unemployment.

We do know some things about what works, and we can draw upon the experience of the New Deal for the unemployed, 25 years ago—one of the most successful interventions ever in terms of active labour market policy. We know that tens of thousands of young people are outside work and learning now, while Welsh employers still report vacancies they struggle to fill. What that tells me is that this isn't only about job preparation; it's structural.

It's no good if a job exists but you never hear about it, or you haven't heard about the young person's guarantee, or you can't afford the bus to reach it, or the bus route doesn't even exist to help you get there. Support on its own is not enough because you cannot train a young person into a job that does not exist. So, you need work on the demand side as well as on the supply side. The work of our new development agency in helping to scale Welsh firms, in building the sectors of the future, and in helping some of our traditional sectors like tourism and food and drink to provide those first jobs, is critical. And we will be asking more of employers. To echo the point that was made by one of the Members here, Governments can do so much, but Governments on their own cannot do everything, and in creating first jobs, we need employers to do more as well.

There's a harder challenge that has been on the horizon and has now arrived. Artificial intelligence, on the early evidence, is not abolishing occupations, but it is stripping out the routine tasks from which entry levels were traditionally built in administration, in customer service, in junior professional work. If firms do not redesign the first rung, it will simply disappear. Our responsibility as a Government is to help make sure that technological change expands opportunity rather than narrows it, and we need the skills system to enable us to do that. Our support right across Government must answer the labour market of tomorrow, not the one of 10 or 15 years ago.

None of this works if a young person cannot find the way in. Too often, we ask the young people that are furthest away from the labour market to navigate the most fragmented part of our public services. Trusted relationships help a young person back into the system: youth services, councils, employers, colleges, trade unions, community organisations. Our job is to make those connections simpler and stronger so that no young person has to tell their story twice.

Llywydd, fair work gives more than a wage; it gives purpose, routine, a place amongst others, community. We'll keep testing what works. We'll ground that in the evidence and the lived experience of young people. We'll be honest about what does not. We'll change course where the evidence demands it. Our focus will be relentlessly on outcomes, not just activity, and the test of everything is simple: whether we reach that 19-year-old in Rhyl sooner, offer them something worth taking, and build a first rung that holds. Diolch.

What I would say is that, in terms of public procurement, specifically—

contributions.text_english: The next item is item 7, the Reform UK debate on bovine TB. And I call on Laura Anne Jones to move the motion.
contributions.text_original: Yr eitem nesaf yw eitem 7, dadl Reform UK—TB buchol. Galwaf ar Laura Anne Jones i wneud y cynnig.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move our Reform motion today in the name of Llŷr Powell.

This has been a long time coming. I believe that, finally, we have the consensus across this Chamber on how we need to and why we need to tackle this cruel bovine TB disease once and for all. I do so in the spirit of seriousness and responsibility, having seen grown men and women, farmers, on their knees crying due to their cattle being slaughtered by previous Governments' failure to tackle this devastating disease.

Bovine TB is not a party political problem. It is one of the top and one of the most pressing and painful issues facing our agricultural communities still today—not according to just me or my party, but according to the entire rural communities across Wales. When I was first elected to this place in 2003, bovine TB was already devastating Welsh farms and had cast a dark cloud over the industry. Over two decades later, farmers are still living under that same dark cloud, watching healthy cattle taken away, enduring endless restrictions and seeing family businesses and family members pushed to breaking point. I think we can all agree across this Chamber that the present strategy and past strategies have not worked. We cannot keep doing the same thing and expecting different results. We all know what needs doing. Our farmers are calling for a fresh start on this, and a bolder, targeted approach led by science.

This disease causes enormous financial damage, but the emotional toll is harder to measure. Coming from a farming family and community in Monmouthshire, I have seen the reality. I've seen the pain and the hardship it causes—watching cattle they have bred, reared and cared for being taken away to be slaughtered, in many cases unnecessarily. And on that, tests have to be improved. They have to be clearer. They have to be more accurate. For those who haven't seen it in their own communities, they may have seen the recent Clarkson's Farm episode of a cow being taken away for slaughter that was carrying twin calves, which were also killed, because of a test that came back as inconclusive, not definitive.

This is the cruel reality of what our farmers are having to deal with. And this isn't a stand-alone case. The toll that this has taken on some of our Welsh farmers has led them to take their own lives. It is not only the cost to human lives, but the cost to animal lives that must be considered. We must also account for the enormous cost to the public purse. Minister, how much has bovine TB cost Wales every year? How much has decades of failure to tackle this disease already cost the Welsh taxpayer, and how much more will it cost Wales if your Government follows in the previous footsteps of past Governments by failing to do what's necessary?

contributions.text_english:
We also recognise in our motion that wildlife is a source of infection, and that's what's been the missing action. Along with higher standards and everything else that farmers accept, it is a significant part of the problem that now, finally, needs to be addressed. Too often, farmers are falsely portrayed as if they do not care about animal welfare or the environment; nothing could be further from the truth. Welsh farmers are amongst our greatest animal lovers and environmental custodians. They do not want to see any animal killed unnecessarily. Our motion recognises the complexity of bovine TB, with the multiple routes of transmission, as well as the infection from wildlife, but we must recognise and accept that wildlife is a source of infection.

We need to incorporate culling in our plan, but, unlike England, we want to see a more targeted, science-led approach that will identify only wildlife and sets that have TB, not a blanket approach, targeting all sets. This, of course, will save wildlife and save unnecessary killing, and also it will help eradicate the disease arguably better than with the approach in England. If the technical advisory group recommends it, that recommendation must be given full consideration—it just must. The evidence already out there shows that this is likely to be a key element for success in ridding Wales of this cruel disease once and for all.

I'm sure you'd agree, Minister, that we need to look at, firstly, focusing these wildlife control efforts in areas with the highest level of bovine TB disease—in Monmouthshire, Pembrokeshire, Ceredigion and so forth. Local evidence showing us where this disease is prevalent should be used to identify those sets and show us where the action is necessary. This will, in turn, protect healthy badger populations, safeguard and save healthy cattle and give farmers in the worst affected areas and communities a chance to break that cycle of infection.

For years, after successive Labour Governments, farmers were given strategies, consultation reviews and warm words, and Labour's amendment today shows that they have still not learned that lesson. After 27 years in Government, nearly three decades of failure in tackling this disease, they want the Chamber to congratulate them for a so-called partnership approach and point to statistics suggesting it's improving. But I invite those who feel this way to attend livestock farms, to visit farms and actually listen to farmers, as everyone across Wales wants bovine TB gone for good, recognising the devastation it causes and the urgency to tackle this.

Farmers living through repeated breakdowns, restrictions and slaughter of healthy cattle will not recognise the rosy picture that you present. We are calling for a targeted, evidence-led approach in areas where bovine TB is most severe. Farmers have already paid too high a price for previous Governments not taking that action. They need a plan that works, they need a timetable. Let's be bold with our aims. Let's try to stop cattle, badgers and wildlife having to die unnecessary and painful deaths from TB.

We now have a Minister that agrees that we can no longer skirt around what we all know to be true—that wildlife is part of that problem. We now have a Minister who has said in this Chamber that he would not be afraid to take those difficult decisions if that's what the science points to. We now, finally, have consensus and an agreement across this Chamber that an urgent, different approach needs to be taken to rid Wales of bovine TB. The majority of us agree now that we need a targeted approach and that we need to take these difficult decisions to protect wildlife, save healthy badgers, healthy cattle, and save our farmers from further mental torture.

This is it. This is the time. This is the Senedd to make a significant difference to our farmers and our rural communities. Minister, if you back our motion today and you heed the cry from our rural communities who need real action, Reform, and other parties in this Chamber, I know, will back you, and we will be behind you 100 per cent. We have a responsibility to do this for future generations, and the ultimate responsibility, of course, lies on your shoulders. I hope today that you'll use this opportunity to state your clear intentions, to make an announcement with firm, clear plans and a timetable for action. We are grateful for your warm words to date on this, Minister, but now is that time for action. Let us be the Senedd and you be the Government to change this. I urge you to all come together across the Chamber today, ahead of the Royal Welsh Show next week, and the local shows in your constituencies this summer, and vote collectively for a motion that will send a strong, reassuring message to our agricultural industry that we are ready to take those tough, grown-up decisions, based in reality and science, that will mean we can finally support our farmers, save animals and rid Wales of this cruel disease once and for all. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: I have selected the amendment to the motion, and I call on Vikki Howells to move amendment 1, tabled in the name of Lynne Neagle. Vikki Howells.
contributions.text_original: Rwyf wedi dethol y gwelliant i'r cynnig. Galwaf ar Vikki Howells i gynnig gwelliant 1, a gyflwynwyd yn enw Lynne Neagle. Vikki Howells.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd, and I formally move the amendment. I'll start by addressing the one element of Reform's motion that Welsh Labour wholeheartedly agrees with and that we don't seek to amend, and that's the effect on farmers, their families and farming communities when a herd has a breakdown. We recognise the emotional and financial impact this, the sheer devastation and the longer term consequences of dealing with this status. So, it's important that we are honest with farmers and farming communities, that we take measures that will make things better for them and not take measures that won't have an impact. And that's the case with some of the items contained in Reform's motion, and I will take some time to explore these.

Point 2: whilst bTB is a complex disease and there are multiple routes by which it can be transmitted, not all routes are equal. The main transmission overwhelmingly is between cattle. That makes up 94 per cent of infection in herds—19 out of 20 cases.

Point 3: I'm sorry for any loss of faith in the previous Welsh Government's approach, but our amendment serves as a reminder of that partnership approach based on tackling cattle-to-cattle transmission taken by the previous Government, working together with farmers and with vets. It delivered and is delivering positive outcomes. Herd prevalence of bTB currently stands at its lowest value since January 2017. The number of new herd instances has more than halved. Almost 95 per cent of herds in Wales are currently free from bTB, and the number of cattle slaughtered has reduced by over a fifth. Of course, there's always more that can be done, and we need to do that, building on the evidence base, but we need to recognise that we are building on solid foundations.

I'm grateful to Laura Anne Jones for clarifying in the Chamber today that she is talking about a targeted approach rather than mass culling, but I do want to also say that there is no faith in mass culling. Three out of five members of the public are against a mass cull and even more are against the notion of spending, wasting public money on a mass cull. I'd note that such an approach, if adopted, would fritter away financing that could otherwise be used to support farmers or the interventions that really would make a difference. And in this vein, I'm sure we can all remember the ludicrous comments of a former Tory environment Secretary justifying the failure of a cull in England by saying badgers moved the goalposts. Hardly comments on which to base confidence or public policy.

That brings us on to point 4. It makes lots of reference to the TB technical advisory group, and that's good. It was the previous Welsh Labour Government that established this body, and it's good to see confidence in it from Reform, and I hope from across the Chamber as well. But more than that, we must remember the advisory group's position, namely that more evidence is needed before any change in policy should be considered, and that this should be done without political interference. Taking a broader view of the science must underpin our decision making on this subject. So, there is one key point that I would like to stress: there is simply no scientific consensus that the culling of wildlife, of badgers, is effective in dealing with bTB. There is a growing number of recent peer-reviewed studies that have considered the impact of badger culling in England, and these studies draw on two principal conclusions: badger culling is ineffective in reducing bTB in cattle and that badgers are not the source or the reservoir of the disease. I expect to hear mention in the Chamber today—

I think, James, you're quoting from Birch et al and Downs et al, which I know has been referenced in some of the stakeholder documents that have been sent to us today. But the Royal Society for the Protection of Cruelty to Animals' conclusion is that those studies conflate badger culling and other measures aimed at cattle, and that the authors acknowledge that they were unable to determine whether badger culling is effective in reducing bTB in cattle. That's why we need this steering group to really look at the scientific evidence in the round.

Progress has been made by earlier and more sensitive cattle testing, improved movement controls, enhanced biosecurity and improved herd management, with better Government support to farmers. We know there's a highly effective vaccine; it's the same one used in humans. With the bulk of bTB transmission being cattle to cattle, I'm interested to see what our technical advisory group says regarding more widespread use of vaccine in herds, the practicalities of this and how those costs might be borne.

So, Llywydd, I will conclude by saying to Plaid Cymru MSs in particular that I know that many of you are passionate about our environment, protecting it and nurturing it so that it can be enjoyed by future generations, and I believe that Reform's motion, with its suggestions of slaughter in the countryside, not based on scientific evidence, will not achieve this. Diolch.

As one of the Members for Gwynedd Maldwyn, I have the privilege of representing one of the largest and most rural constituencies in Wales, where agriculture is the backbone of our economy and our communities, and I'm therefore grateful to speak in support of this motion. Before today's debate, I wanted to hear not from officials or policy papers, but from people living with bovine TB every day. So, over the weekend, I met with farmers from across Montgomeryshire. What those farmers told me was not just about cattle—it was about the emotional, financial and human cost of living under the constant shadow of bovine TB.

According to the latest NFU statistics, in the year to December 2024, there were 500 new bovine TB herd incidents across Wales, and more than 10,000 cattle were slaughtered as part of TB control. They're not just statistics. They represent hundreds of farming businesses, and thousands of difficult conversations around kitchen tables across rural Wales. When we debate bovine TB, it is easy to become consumed by statistics, testing regimes and policy arguments. Those things matter, but we should never lose sight of the people living through the disease every single day.

The farmers I met were not asking for sympathy. They were asking for certainty. They were asking for leadership. Farmers from across the Tanat, Vyrnwy and Severn valleys described living with the constant worry that the next routine test could change everything. Some also told me they had reduced their cattle numbers or moved away from keeping cattle altogether, because they simply could not continue living with the uncertainty and risk of prolonged TB restrictions. That should concern every Member of this Senedd. If farmers are changing the very nature of their business because of the fear of bovine TB, then the impact of this disease extends far beyond the individual farm.

When TB is detected, beef farmers can no longer sell their cattle freely. Dairy farmers continue producing milk, but movement restrictions still disrupt their businesses and make it difficult to plan for the future. The impact, however, goes far beyond the balance sheet. Farmers can prepare for bad weather. They can prepare for difficult markets. What they cannot prepare for is the uncertainty of not knowing whether the next routine test will change everything. Every TB test brings back the same question, 'What if this one comes back positive?' That uncertainty affects mental well-being, family life and confidence in the future. It creates sleepless nights and constant anxiety over whether the business will withstand another breakdown.

One of the most difficult conversations I had was with a farmer who described the reality of having to slaughter a recently-calved cow on the farm because of bovine TB restrictions. That is something no livestock keeper ever wants to experience. It is a stark reminder that behind every policy and every statistic are real people making heartbreaking decisions about animals they have cared for every day.

The farmers also made another point that struck me: whilst vets and testers are rightly paid for carrying out the testing regime, farmers themselves receive nothing for the considerable time spent gathering the livestock, handling the cattle and dealing with the disruption. That time has a financial cost.

The effects don't stop at the farm gate, either. Agriculture sustains livestock markets, feed merchants, agriculture suppliers, contractors, hauliers, machinery dealers and many other rural businesses. When a farm suffers a prolonged TB breakdown, the effects ripple through the whole rural economy. Llywydd, if our shared objective is the eradication of bovine TB—and I believe that is something every Member in this Chamber shares—then we have a duty to ask a simple question: is the current approach delivering that objective? If not, we have a responsibility to examine every source of infection, and every scientifically validated control method available to us. Whatever recommendations are ultimately made by the TB technical advisory group, I believe the Welsh Government has a duty to consider them objectively, proportionately, and on the basis of the available evidence. That's not ideology; it's good policy.

Behind every herd restriction is a farming family carrying an enormous emotional and financial burden. Behind every positive test is another difficult conversation around the kitchen table. Behind every statistic is a farming family trying to plan for the future. Some are now questioning whether they continue keeping cattle, and that should concern every one of us. Because, if cattle leave our farms, the effects are felt throughout the wider rural economy. Our decisions today don't just affect cattle. They affect people, they affect families, they affect livelihoods, and they affect the future of our rural communities.

Llywydd, farmers can live with many challenges: bad weather, volatile markets and rising costs. What they cannot live with is indefinite uncertainty. They deserve confidence that Wales is serious about eradicating bovine TB and prepared to follow the evidence wherever it leads. For the sake of our farmers, their families, and the generations that will follow, I urge Members across this Chamber to support this motion. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Could I say, as the son of a farmer, that I was very aware of the effects of TB. TB casts a long shadow over our cattle farmers and dairy producers and our rural communities, and it's one of the main barriers to achieving a Welsh agricultural industry that is productive, progressive and profitable. Having TB on a farm affects all aspects of day-to-day farm management. It affects the marketing of animals, such as the sale of store cattle, breeding animals and calves, which leads to additional costs, additional food, feed, shelter, grazing and so forth.

The loss of productive and breeding cattle due to TB negatively effects the yield, for example, fewer litres of milk, and the productivity of the farm, for example through the loss of genetic potential. TB outbreaks result in significant financial and emotional stress for farmers and families. According to the latest statistics available, throughout Wales during the period from April 2025 to March 2026, 10,395 cattle were slaughtered due to TB. More than 14,000 herd tests were carried out, nearly 2 million individual cattle tests were carried out, and 479 new herd events were detected. These statistics provide little comfort to farmers across the country, who continue to live with this terrible disease. It's worth noting that almost two thirds of the animals that would end up being slaughtered due to TB in Wales over the last 12-month reporting period were in the high TB area in the west, namely Pembrokeshire and parts of Carmarthenshire and Ceredigion, highlighting the regional variation in the disease.

We have to also realise that farmers have a high suicide rate, with up to one case per week. A survey of farmers shows that the majority believe that poor mental health is the biggest problem in agriculture. Around 64 per cent of farmers surveyed by Farmers Weekly feel positive about their physical health, but only 55 per cent of farmers feel positive about their mental health. Cases of infection increase stress.

Fifty per cent of farmers surveyed by the Farming Community Network were dismayed or concerned about TB. Some farmers believe that the public don't understand the challenges of farming and feel underappreciated. Thank goodness that Samaritans Wales is aiming to break the cycle of suicide risk in rural Wales by launching the Our Farming, Our Future project. The partnership forged with the farming support charity Tir Dewi works closely with the Wales Federation of Young Farmers Clubs and its members to develop peer-led resources and activities that can be used and shared in all clubs, with the ultimate aim of reducing the risk of suicide in rural communities throughout Wales, and thanks to them for their work.

By the end of the 1960s, the presence of TB in cattle in the UK had almost disappeared. By the mid-1970s, all herds in the UK had been cleansed of the disease, though not all at the same time. We must accept disease control policies that are evidence based, transparent and demonstrably effective. In March 2023, the previous Welsh Government launched a five-year action plan that set out the future policy direction for the TB eradication programme. The bovine TB technical advisory group was established in April 2024 as part of governance reforms set out in the action plan. TAG provides independent expert scientific and technical advice to Welsh Ministers and senior officials on the TB eradication programme and brings together different strands of technical and practical expertise to provide that advice. Its membership includes some of the world's leading experts in science, epidemiology and bovine TB immunology, and that's something that we should all be proud of. And so, in exactly the same way that scientific evidence is used to spur action on the challenges of climate change, we must act on the basis of scientific evidence in relation to TB. That is why we must listen to, read, understand and respect the work of the panel in due course—a body that was established, when all is said and done, by the previous Labour Government. Thank you very much.

Mae colli buchod cynhyrchiol a magu yn sgil TB yn effeithio'n negyddol ar y cynnyrch, er enghraifft, llai o litrau o laeth, a chynhyrchiant y fferm, er enghraifft trwy golli potensial genetig. Mae'r haint yn cynyddu’r straen.

Roedd 50 y cant o ffermwyr a holwyd gan Rwydwaith Cymuned Ffermio wedi'u siomi gan neu'n poeni am TB. Mae rhai ffermwyr yn meddwl nad yw'r cyhoedd yn deall heriau ffermio ac yn teimlo eu bod yn cael eu tanwerthfawrogi. Diolch byth, mae Samariaid Cymru yn ceisio torri'r cylch risg hunanladdiad yng nghefn gwlad Cymru drwy brosiect Ein Ffermio, Ein Dyfodol. Mae'r bartneriaeth â'r elusen cymorth ffermio Tir Dewi yn gweithio'n agos gyda chlybiau ffermwyr ifanc Cymru a'u haelodau i ddatblygu adnoddau a gweithgareddau a arweinir gan gymheiriaid a all gael eu defnyddio a'u rhannu ym mhob clwb, gyda'r bwriad yn y pen draw o leihau'r risg o hunanladdiad mewn cymunedau gwledig ledled Cymru, a diolch iddynt am eu gwaith.

Erbyn diwedd y 1960au, roedd presenoldeb TB mewn gwartheg yn y Deyrnas Unedig bron iawn â diflannu. Erbyn canol y 1970au, roedd pob buches yn y Deyrnas Unedig wedi cael eu glanhau o'r clwyf, er nad ar yr un pryd. Rhaid derbyn polisïau rheoli clefydau sydd wedi'u seilio ar dystiolaeth, yn dryloyw ac yn amlwg yn effeithiol. Ym mis Mawrth 2023, lansiodd y Llywodraeth Cymru flaenorol gynllun gweithredu pum mlynedd a nododd gyfeiriad polisi'r dyfodol ar gyfer rhaglen dileu TB. Sefydlwyd grŵp cynghori technegol TB bovine ym mis Ebrill 2024 fel rhan o ddiwygiadau llywodraethu a bennwyd yn y cynllun gweithredu. Mae TAG yn darparu cyngor gwyddonol a thechnegol arbenigol annibynnol i Weinidogion Cymru ac i uwch swyddogion ar raglen dileu TB ac yn dod â gwahanol arbenigedd technegol ac ymarferol at ei gilydd i roi'r cyngor hwnnw. Mae aelodaeth yn cynnwys rhai o'r arbenigwyr gorau yn y byd ym maes gwyddoniaeth epidemioleg ac imiwnoleg, ac mae'n rhywbeth y dylen ni i gyd ymfalchïo ynddo. Ac felly, yn union yr un modd a ddefnyddir tystiolaeth wyddonol i gael gweithredu ar heriau newid hinsawdd, rhaid gweithredu ar sail dystiolaeth wyddonol mewn perthynas â TB. Dyna pam rhaid gwrando, darllen, deall a pharchu gwaith y panel maes o law—un a sefydlwyd, ar ddiwedd y dydd, gan Lywodraeth Lafur flaenorol. Diolch yn fawr.

I think everybody in the Siambr agrees on one thing: nobody wants bovine TB to be a part of Welsh farming in another 10 or 20 years' time. Whatever our views on how we get there, we all want to see this disease managed more effectively, not only in cattle, but in the general wildlife population as well. The difficulty is that farmers have been hearing that ambition for a very long time, yet, if you speak to them today, the majority don't feel like we're getting any closer to the long-term goal of eradicating the disease. Farmers still live with the same uncertainty, the same movement restrictions and the same crippling anxiety every time a test comes around. They still see healthy, productive cattle being slaughtered. I can't put into words just how distressing it is for me to read the latest data. Over 10,000 cattle were slaughtered in Wales last year alone, with 479 new herd incidents detected—479. My heart goes out to every person doing their best to cope with the mental strain caused by bovine TB. That is why Reform has brought this debate forward today, because we don't think it's good enough to simply carry on with the same conversation we've been having for years and expect farmers to believe that something is about to change.

One thing that has struck me over the last few weeks, and, indeed, during the election campaign, is that I've listened to Plaid Cymru say that they will follow the science. I don't disagree with that. In fact, that's exactly what the Government should be doing. But I keep coming back to the same question: follow the science to where? This isn't a new disease. We're not starting from scratch. Welsh Governments have had years of evidence available to them. They've had scientific advice. They've had the technical advisory group. They've had veterinary expertise, years of surveillance data and years of lived experience from the farmers themselves. Farmers in my constituency aren't asking whether the Government has enough evidence yet. They're asking what the Government has actually concluded from the scientific evidence it already has. Evidence doesn't make decisions; Ministers do. And this current Minister has years of experience in opposition. He knows better than anyone exactly what the science is telling him. At some point, this Government has to demonstrate what it has learned from the evidence it has spent years collecting, and that it's ready to harness that data and take meaningful, tangible steps to manage bovine TB in Wales.

I find myself thinking back to what Plaid Cymru used to say when they sat on the opposition benches. Llyr Gruffydd spoke passionately about bovine TB, he challenged Labour's approach, he spoke about the pressure on farming families and questioned whether the existing strategy was delivering what farmers had been promised. He spoke about the need to listen to the evidence and to the industry. Those were perfectly legitimate questions to ask and they're just as legitimate now that Plaid Cymru is in Government.

Farmers don’t see politics in the way we do. They don’t look at which benches people are sitting on; they simply want to know whether anything is going to actually change. What is this Senedd doing to help them, to make their lives easier and to give the next generation of farmers a future? If the answer is that we need more time, I suspect many farmers will say they've already given successive Governments enough time. If the answer is another review, they'll say that we've had reviews before. If the answer is more evidence, they'll quite reasonably ask what happened to all the evidence that we've already gathered. That isn't an argument against science—quite the opposite; it's an argument for having the confidence to act on the science.

I've never accepted that this debate should be reduced to people choosing sides before they've even discussed the evidence. Whether it's cattle controls, biosecurity, vaccination or a controlled wildlife cull, surely the starting point has to be an honest assessment of what is and isn't working. Because if we can't ask those questions now, after everything farmers have lived through, when can we?

The uncomfortable reality is that, after decades of increasingly stringent cattle controls, Wales is still recording thousands of reactor cattle every year and hundreds of new herd incidents. It is entirely reasonable to ask whether the strategy, taken as a whole, is getting us where we all want to be. I don't think that it's a criticism of farmers—quite the opposite; farmers have done what successive Governments have asked of them. They have accepted tighter controls, greater costs and more bureaucracy, because they believed they were contributing towards better management of the disease. Government now has to show the same willingness to examine its own approach, because—[Interruption.] No, I'd like to make progress. Behind every statistic is a family trying to make a living; behind every breakdown are years of breeding, investment and hard work. I don't believe farmers expect miracles, they know that this is one of the most difficult animal health challenges we face, but they do expect leadership, especially when the Minister talked such a good game in opposition.

With all due respect—and I say this as constructively as possible—does the Minister want his legacy in Government to be that of a doer, or does he want to be remembered as a talker or a promiser? Talk is cheap, farmers are clear: they don't want hope, they want action. Diolch yn fawr.

Bovine TB continues to be one of the most pressing issues facing farmers in Ceredigion Penfro, and the message that I continue to hear from local farmers is absolutely clear. They want to see meaningful action to tackle this disease. Among those affected are my own in-laws, whose farm has been affected by bovine TB for more than two decades. And so, I declare an interest, as through their experience, I've seen first-hand the profound emotional, practical and financial toll that bovine TB continues to have on farming families. Their story is similar to that of many other farmers in my constituency, and together, they reiterate the need for effective measures to address this long-standing issue.

As has already been said, it is heartbreaking. The dread and worry over testing, the anguish and stress over a TB breakdown and subsequent slaughter, and, of course, the anxiety of dealing with compensation payments and trying to run a sustainable business. An NFU Cymru survey in 2023 highlighted that 85 per cent of respondents said bovine TB had negatively impacted their own mental health or someone in their family, and over 93 per cent said that they were extremely concerned or very concerned about bovine TB. So, I really hope that with a new Government and with a Cabinet Minister sympathetic to farmers and the anguish they are going through because of bovine TB, I hope action will now be taken to finally get to grips with this awful disease.

As the second point in the motion notes, there must be a recognition of the multiple routes of transmission, including infection from wildlife. In the last Senedd, I had the privilege of chairing the Economy, Trade and Rural Affairs Committee and we held an inquiry into the Welsh Government's bovine TB eradication programme. The committee made some important recommendations in areas like testing, compensation, and even wildlife. The committee was concerned about the lack of data around the role of wildlife in spreading bovine TB, but the reality is that you can't possibly control the disease without dealing with the wildlife reservoir.

We all recognise that there are multiple mechanisms of transmission, and even the previous Welsh Government accepted that in their response to the committee, which is why there needs to be a package of measures that deals with all types of transmission of this disease. The previous Government told the committee that it's not really so much about understanding the mechanisms of transmission in greater detail, as we know they occur, but more about understanding the relative frequency with which they occur and why they occur in different local situations.

So, if we all accept that there is transmission via wildlife, why has there been an absence of efforts to address this in the first place? This cannot be the case going forward. The Cabinet Minister himself has said that wildlife is part of the bovine TB problem and must be part of the solution, and now he's in a position to actually do something about it. Farmers across Wales are watching, and they are tired of having to tell us the same thing over and over again. They now want action.

From April 2025 to March 2026, 3,068 cattle were slaughtered in Pembrokeshire and a further 971 in Ceredigion. That's over 4,000 cattle slaughtered in just two counties over a 12-month period. When I was first elected in 2007, that figure for Pembrokeshire was 2,384 and for Ceredigion was just 296. Of course, testing is far more sensitive than it was back then, but that is still a huge increase in cattle slaughtered, and behind each slaughter is a farming family devastated by it, which is why I've campaigned on this specific issue for the last 20 years.

Llywydd, the Welsh Conservatives will be supporting the motion this afternoon, even though we do not believe the motion is strong enough. However, in the interests of consensus and in order to push this matter forward, we will be voting for the motion. The motion states that in the event that the TB technical advisory group recommends targeted wildlife control, including culling, such recommendations are given full and proper consideration. Well, I believe that the evidence is already there to show that this disease needs to be tackled in the wildlife reservoir, and so I do not believe we need to wait for further information and advice before any actual action takes place.

We of course support maintaining robust biosecurity standards, but the Welsh Government must use all the tools in its box to tackle all transmissions of this disease. Llywydd, we want to see the Welsh Government get on with the job of eradicating bovine TB. There have been endless discussions about whether to introduce a holistic approach or not, and we believe the time for talking is now over. We now want action.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Presiding Officer. Now, for some, this is handkerchiefs out time, because we need to talk about badgers and deer, both of which feature on the cuddly part of the animal spectrum, though I do notice that we have quite a few empty seats.

I looked at some of the data on this, and I have to say, initially, when I looked at England and Wales, the data looked remarkably similar, and I thought, what's the issue? But then I looked at Scotland, and Scotland's really, really interesting. And then I looked at the regions of England, and I looked at the regions of Wales, and a light came on. I could see myself directly what the problem was.

It's strange that some matters have become bizarrely and wrongly a matter of left and right, for example, bin collections and speed limits. For some reason, badgers fall into that category. It shouldn't be the case. Those in this Chamber who are perhaps vegans have a perfectly valid argument to deploy: there should be no cattle in the countryside, as they exist only for our benefit as consumers. No cattle, no badger problem. But for those of us who enjoy dairy products and meat and use leather, we know that there is a trade-off between our wishes and wildlife. The countryside that gives us a delight to be in is rarely natural. It has been created by our farmers over hundreds of years. They do a remarkable job, and we should listen to them.

In a perfect world, we'd have a reliable test for bovine TB. We'd have a proven vaccination for bovine TB, which we'd use in cattle, relatively easily, and in wildlife, which is a bit more difficult to achieve. But we don't have any of that yet, so we have to deal with the situation as we find it. The facts are that in some parts of Wales bovine TB is explosive. It is true that cattle are more likely to catch it from other members of the herd, but it's also true that the first infected in the herd is likely to become infected from wildlife, and there's a clear link between the number of badgers and infection. Scotland is largely clear of bovine TB and has a very low badger population. There's evidence from England that culling badgers in those TB reservoir areas substantially reduces cases after four years.

Food security should be at the forefront of all our minds, not to mention the risk of losing rare bloodlines and losing farmers with extensive knowledge and skills in dairy and beef. We should be working with farmers and vets to ensure that all diseased animals are culled early, but no matter what your view or how you came to it, the fact remains that bovines and badgers cohabit. Much effort and paperwork goes into testing cattle pre and post movement. Unfortunately, somebody forgot to send the badgers the memorandum about not moving around. In the real world, strategic culling within these wildlife reservoirs has to form part of TB management, at least for now.

This is a Reform UK motion, but it's a motion to help Welsh farmers. It is an example how this expanded Senedd can work together for the good of Wales. Please support it.

contributions.text_english:
I want to begin by recognising the profound impact, as others have done in this Chamber, that bovine TB continues to have on farming families and on rural communities across Wales. It impacts on people and animal welfare alike. For too many of my constituents in Ceredigion Penfro, this is a daily reality. Time and again, farmers have spoken to me about the emotional and financial strain that bovine TB places on their businesses and their families. Only last week, one constituent told me that they had been forced to cull around 600 cattle because of the disease. Sadly, theirs is far from an isolated case.

Across Ceredigion Penfro, farmers are making heartbreaking decisions that carry enormous financial consequences and take a significant toll on their mental well-being. For some, these pressures have become so overwhelming that they are questioning whether they can carry on in the industry at all. Bovine TB remains one of the greatest challenges facing agriculture in my constituency. Alongside economic consequences, we must acknowledge the human cost. The stress, uncertainty and anxiety experienced by farming families living under prolonged TB restrictions cannot simply be measured in financial terms.

S4C's Ffermio highlighted these realities powerfully, reminding us that behind every statistic are people, families and communities living with the consequences of this disease. I understand this can be a difficult and emotive subject, but I urge everybody in the Chamber to avoid the temptation to use this to polarise debate or for political point-scoring. Precisely because it is so important and so complex, our response must be guided by the evidence. This is not a black-and-white issue. There is no one-size-fits-all answer. The science is not static, and we have to be ready to be responsive to new developments and innovations, as well as what we have learned from past programmes. So, I urge this Government to remain open to considering every measure that can contribute to eradicating bovine TB.

That is why I look forward to receiving the recommendations of the bovine TB technical advisory group, and I welcome the emphasis in this motion that full and proper consideration needs to be given to any recommendations coming from this group, although I do note that the Reform Member seems not to agree with that aspect of the motion. Progress by the previous Labour Government was painfully slow. Without significant change, the bovine TB programme board has said that Wales will not eradicate bovine TB by 2041, and that should concern every Member of the Senedd.

People on all sides of this debate want progress, not political point-scoring. They want confidence that decisions are being taken because they're effective, proportionate and evidence-led. They want a Government willing to make difficult decisions where necessary, knowing that these have been taken following careful and balanced consideration, something I have full confidence that this Government will do.

For my constituency, this debate is particularly significant. Around two-thirds of all cattle slaughtered because of bovine TB in Wales last year were in high TB area west, covering the whole of Pembrokeshire and parts of Ceredigion, as Paul Davies has mentioned. That underlines the need for action that reflects the realities on the ground. A one-size-fits-all approach will not deliver eradication. We need targeted, science-led interventions, involving farmers and vets and other stakeholders as part of a wide strategy to finally eradicate bovine TB. For those reasons, I will support the motion today. 

I welcome the Minister's clear commitment to eradicating TB for the benefit of people, the economy and wildlife alike, and I urge the Minister now to keep his clear focus on achieving that outcome. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Bovine TB is the cause of so much pain, trauma and uncertainty for farmers and the rural communities of Wales. I am, however, very concerned about the unhelpful and untimely political posturing of the motion, as well as the misleading inferences contained in the wording. The motion calls on the Welsh Government to draw on the scientific evidence, and rightly so, but the motion also appears to imply that a major component of the solution should be a badger cull. Since the previous Welsh Government announced its decision to stop culling badgers back in March 2012, the number of new herd incidents has more than halved, and bovine TB is now at its lowest level in nearly 20 years. All of this has been achieved without any lethal wildlife control. 

As we've heard, the evidence shows that 94 per cent of bovine TB transmission occurs from cattle to cattle. This is where the solutions lie and where improved testing and biosecurity measures have already made a real difference. The technical advisory group is currently considering the evidence relevant to vaccination and bovine TB. The Cabinet Minister recently acknowledged this research and reminded us of the importance of allowing this work to be completed before any decisions are made. The timing of this debate, ahead of the publication of these findings, is therefore premature. So, I urge Members to vote against the motion and in favour of the amendment in order that the evidence presented by the technical advisory group can be given proper consideration at the appropriate time. The group's work is politically independent and must remain so for a robust science-led approach to be maintained. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
There's no doubt that bovine TB is a highly complex, challenging and persistent disease. There is no single route of transmission and no simple solution. Cattle-to-cattle transmission remains a significant issue, but it is recognised that wildlife can also act as a source of infection, and that is why our response must be comprehensive and based on the evidence. As Members know, I recently announced my intention to refresh the TB eradication programme. The foundations of the current programme are strong, but we all now need to build on that progress and all step up our efforts if we're to achieve our ambition of a TB-free Wales by 2041.

I've met with the farming unions, with the British Veterinary Association, the TB programme board and the chair of the technical advisory group. Along with the wider technical advisory group membership, their combined expertise and advice will help shape the next phase of our approach. I agree that robust biosecurity standards and practices must remain a cornerstone of on-farm disease control. Effective biosecurity is a shared responsibility, with farmers and veterinarians working in partnership to prevent, detect and respond to disease threats, protecting animal health, livelihoods, public health and the resilience of our farms. But we must also be honest with ourselves. While biosecurity and cattle controls are essential, they're not the whole answer. If we are serious about achieving a TB-free Wales, we have to consider all sources of infection and all scientifically validated control measures available to us. This is why I agree that any future approach must recognise wildlife as one of several sources of infection that can contribute to the spread of bovine TB.

While I recognise that wildlife can play a role in the transmission of bovine TB, it is important that we don't pretend that wildlife is responsible in every case, nor should we prejudge the conclusions of our expert advisors. The technical advisory group is there to provide independent scientific expertise and advice, while the programme board brings together a wealth of practical lived experience and expertise from across the sector. I'm currently awaiting further advice from both groups on the role of wildlife and wildlife interventions, amongst other topics, and I look forward to considering the evidence base and their advice carefully. I also intend, by the way, to publish that advice to inform the wider debate.

I understand the frustrations of those who believe that progress has not been fast enough, and yes, I share those frustrations as much as anyone else. However, it is important that we get this right and that our decisions are grounded in robust evidence, alongside consideration of effectiveness, practicality, deliverability, animal welfare and value for money for the taxpayer. We must also recognise that some progress has been made in Wales. Let's not forget that more than 95 per cent of Welsh herds are officially TB free. That, I have to say, reflects the substantial efforts and hard work of farmers themselves, the vets that they work with and officials across Wales. I think we should always recognise that those efforts are ongoing.

But the challenge we face now is to build on that progress and push forward towards TB eradication in Wales. Innovative projects in Pembrokeshire and north Wales, for example, demonstrate the value of collaboration, stronger engagement between farmers and their vets, and local tailored action. I know that just as no two farms are the same, no two herd TB breakdowns are the same, and the measures to keep TB out of individual herds will also be different again. I commend the work of both of these projects and recognise the positive feedback that they're generating. The knowledge and experience from both of those projects will help inform future policy development. Picking up on some comments made about us knowing what we need to do and that the evidence is there, as Anna Nicholl told us, the science isn't static. That's why we have brought scientists, vets and world-renowned experts together in the form of the technical advisory group. They've travelled halfway around the world to come to Wales to help us deal with this situation, and it's constantly evolving. We're constantly learning from those local projects, from experiences in other parts of the UK and beyond. It's only right that we let the experts advise us and not think that politicians know best.

With regard to the proposed amendment, I welcome the constructive approach taken by the Member in recognising that progress has been made over recent years. However, you can't deny that the programme board's position paper, which was published in March, was clear that a step change is needed if we are to meet our TB eradication target here in Wales. Without that, more animals, more farmers, more farming families will experience the distress caused by TB breakdowns for longer.

That, I have to say, reflects the substantial efforts and hard work of farmers themselves, the vets that they work with and officials across Wales. I think we should always recognise that those efforts are ongoing.

But the challenge we face now is to build on that progress and push forward towards TB eradication in Wales. Innovative projects in Pembrokeshire and north Wales, for example, demonstrate the value of collaboration, stronger engagement between farmers and their vets, and local tailored action. I know that just as no two farms are the same, no two herd TB breakdowns are the same, and the measures to keep TB out of individual herds will also be different again. I commend the work of both of these projects and recognise the positive feedback that they're generating. The knowledge and experience from both of those projects will help inform future policy development. Picking up on some comments made about us knowing what we need to do and that the evidence is there, as Anna Nicholl told us, the science isn't static. That's why we have brought scientists, vets and world-renowned experts together in the form of the technical advisory group. They've travelled halfway around the world to come to Wales to help us deal with this situation, and it's constantly evolving. We're constantly learning from those local projects, from experiences in other parts of the UK and beyond. It's only right that we let the experts advise us and not think that politicians know best.

With regard to the proposed amendment, I welcome the constructive approach taken by the Member in recognising that progress has been made over recent years. However, you can't deny that the programme board's position paper, which was published in March, was clear that a step change is needed if we are to meet our TB eradication target here in Wales. Without that, more animals, more farmers, more farming families will experience the distress caused by TB breakdowns for longer.

contributions.text_english: Llywydd, the common enemy here is bovine TB, and our commitment is clear. We will update the TB eradication programme and develop a new science-led, evidence-based and holistic approach, which is collaborative too. We are developing it in a collaborative way. There are no quick fixes, I fear, for TB in cattle, but by working together and focusing on cattle, people and wildlife, I believe that we can accelerate progress and move Wales closer to our shared ambition, an ambition that I know we all share in the Chamber, of eliminating TB by 2041. Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'd like to declare a relevant interest: I have close family who keep cattle. I'd like to thank all Members for their contribution to the debate today, and anyone who is involved in the industry who is watching this and looking for change here, and all those Members who talked about the financial, emotional and human pressures that bovine TB places on our farming families across Wales.

Laura Anne Jones opened the debate saying we finally have a consensus in this Chamber that something needs to be changed. You raised the stress and anxiety that farmers face, but also the economic damage to the industry. But you also talked about the human cost, and the cost it has in lives in the industry as well. And you also highlighted the infected wildlife and that we need a step change here. As the Minister highlighted as well, the programme board has said we do need to have a step change here in Wales. You did also reinforce about previous Governments failing to address the disease, with numerous projects that really didn't get us anywhere, just got us in the mess that we're in now.

Vikki Howells, it was good that you recognised the pressures that the disease placed on farmers. You also say that cattle-to-cattle transmission is high. I don't dispute that, but they've got to get infected from somewhere in the first place, and that tends to be from the wildlife population. You also mentioned the number of incidents going down, but I'd just like to quietly remind you that the herd of cattle across Wales has dropped by 40 per cent, so there's naturally going to be a drop in the numbers of herds getting infected when fewer and fewer people across this country are keeping cattle, for a number of the reasons that Members highlighted today.

You also said that the TAG needed more science and we needed more science again, but we've heard that from previous Labour Governments for a number of years. They know what the science is, but then when they don't like the science advice they're given, they say we need more, and then we need more again. You can't keep asking for more science until you get the answer you want. If the answer is clear from a number of studies, something needs to be done about it.

Andrew Griffin raised the 500 new outbreaks and 10,000 cattle lost every year. That's already at breaking point. The critical numbers of cattle across the country are so low now, that's putting huge pressure on the wider system, like our abattoirs. Other Members talked about the economic elements of that, especially the jobs that we're seeing lost in some of the abattoirs across the country. It all feeds into the reason why people are not keeping more cattle, because of the human impact of this disease. Having continuous testing of cattle all the time puts huge stress on our farmers, but also puts huge stress on the animals, which makes them very dangerous when you're handling them all the time. That is why we're seeing a rise in people getting injured by cattle with continuous TB testing.

Elwyn Vaughan, thank you for your contribution. I know you've talked on this a number of times when we both sat in the chamber of Powys County Council together. You highlighted the mental impacts that this places on families, and also the work that the young farmers clubs are doing across the country, an organisation that really made me come here a lot of the time. You talked about the work that they're doing to support people with their mental health across the country. And I would just say to anybody watching this debate, if you are struggling with your mental health and well-being in the industry, there are a number of charities in the rural sphere who will step in and help you, because no-one should have to suffer alone.

Helen Jenner, you talked about farmers feeling that we need to move on. We've had these discussions, and I can tell you I've probably talked in this Chamber a number of times about TB, probably more than I've talked about anything else here. And we do need to have some movement. It's pleasing to hear that Plaid Cymru will be supporting this motion today from what I'm led to believe, and that is a positive step that we've got a majority now that wants to get on and do something about this. Our farming families have waited far too long, and the time for action is now.

Paul Davies, I'd like to thank you for all the work that you've done on this for 20 years, and I also recognise the impact this has had on your family. I know you've been a champion of this. I know your colleague who was here, Sam Kurtz, raised a project in Pembrokeshire around this and the work that they've done, but also the work that the previous Economy, Trade and Rural Affairs Committee did on this. There was another piece of evidence that I'd like to highlight to Vikki Howells. That was a cross-party report that came back that said we do need to take action in the wildlife. But I need to be clear: this isn't, as people talked about, a blanket cull of wildlife. This is a science-led approach, because anybody who knows anything about this subject will tell you that if you have non-infected badgers, the best thing to do with them is leave them well alone. Some people who've had badgers on their farms for a number of years have never had instances of TB. This is a targeted approach where you can go in and remove infected wildlife. I know other Members talked about a vaccine, but the problem we have with a vaccine is that when you have the testing done, they cannot actually distinguish which animals have been vaccinated and which animals have not. So, the vaccine is not quite there yet, but thanks, Paul, for all that you've done on this.

Stephen Senior, I agree with everything you said about farmers shaping our environment and how they need to be supported, but also the bureaucratic elements that come with TB—the paperwork that comes with it, with case vets and all the people who come around you all time; it's an absolute nuisance and it puts a lot of stress on our farmers.

Thank you, Anna Nicholl, for your powerful contribution, highlighting the Ffermio documentary. I can remember in the previous Senedd when that was highlighted. I don't think anybody across this Chamber could not be moved by what was said on there and the cow that was culled on there that had a calf inside her as well. A lot of people were moved by that. I actually thought the previous Government would move on that. They moved a little bit on policy on it, but it didn't have a huge step change, which we all hoped it would.

Paul Rock, I respect your right to an opinion about infection rates, but I'd like to say what I said earlier, that, actually, the herd rate has gone down by 40 per cent here in Wales, so there's going to be less infections.

We do need action now and I think we need to have a clear steer in this Chamber for the Minister that, if the technical advisory group comes out and says we need to have a targeted intervention in wildlife, the Minister's got a clear steer that the majority of this Chamber want to move that way and not have more posturing and debates to stall the issue. We need to move on.

And, finally, to the Cabinet Secretary—. I think I'm doing all right for time. And, finally, to the Cabinet Minister, I should say, not the Cabinet Secretary—thank you for your response. It's actually very refreshing to hear a Minister sat in that chair actually saying that we need to get on and sort this issue and not defending a failed policy for the last 20-odd years. Because I do agree with you on biosecurity, that this isn't just a one-size-fits-all, and no outbreak is the same. So, we need to make sure we're addressing the biosecurity. Working with vets—I think that's very important—to understand your individual circumstances and put that right, and, hopefully, the Welsh Government, when looking at grants—. They did an awful lot of work, actually, about raising feeders so that people aren't feeding on the floor, making sure that stalls are covered, to make sure we can get this disease under control.

But I would just like to say to the Minister, one thing that probably hasn't been mentioned is about case vets—something that you probably have had raised, and me—making sure there is that consistency with case vets when they are going out on farms, because there's nothing more frustrating for people if they have different vets all the time, and that does cause a lot of anxiety in the industry.

I'd like to thank all Members, and I'm testing the Llywydd's patience, because it's gone red and people want to go home, but I will say 'thank you' to all Members who have contributed today. There is a differing opinion, but I think there is a majority in this Chamber now that wants us to move on this issue. So, I'd just like to thank all Members today. Let's get the step change we need, let's support those farmers and let's get this disease, finally, once and for all, under control. I advise all Members to support the motion.

contributions.text_english: Item 8 next, the Welsh Conservatives debate: the deposit-return scheme. I call on Janet Finch-Saunders to move the motion.
contributions.text_original: Eitem 8 nesaf, dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: cynllun dychwelyd ernes. Galwaf ar Janet Finch-Saunders i wneud y cynnig.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Wales has every reason to be proud of its recycling record. We have the second highest recycling rate in the world, with a national recycling rate of 68.4 per cent. Twelve of Wales's 22 local authorities have already met the Welsh Government's statutory target of recycling 70 per cent of municipal waste, and I have to say, my own local authority, Conwy County Borough Council, get brownie points from me on the fact that they are one of the most successful ones. These achievements are testament to the efforts of our Welsh households, local authorities and businesses, who have embraced recycling and sustainability. That is why the Welsh Conservatives have continuously supported the principle of a deposit-return scheme, because we believe that it can reduce litter, increase recycling rates, encourage responsible behaviour and help protect our environment, our sea mammals and our wildlife.

Now, in 2016, I was incredibly proud to have brought forward a successful legislative proposal for a Bill that would make provisions to introduce a deposit-return scheme and reduce waste in Wales. We're now in 2026. Around the world, successful schemes in countries such as Germany and Norway consistently achieve return rates of over 90 per cent, minimising litter and keeping valuable materials in circulation. So, this debate isn't about whether Wales should have a deposit-return scheme, it's about whether the proposed scheme is fit for purpose, affordable and works for businesses and customers alike. The former Welsh Labour Government chose to create a system that differs from—and this is after 10 years—the rest of the UK by including glass within the scheme, despite all the evidence suggesting it is unworkable. This divergence for the sake of divergence will have very real consequences for the Welsh economy. Wales already collects 92 per cent of glass at the kerbside, so I fail to understand why including glass in the DRS is such a priority for this Plaid Cymru Government. I fear this is shaping up to be yet another Welsh taxpayer-funded disaster.
