contributions.text_english:
The inclusion of glass makes the scheme significantly more complicated and substantially more expensive, as glass requires dedicated collection infrastructure, specialist handing, expensive transportation because of its weight compared to plastic and cans and paper, and more costly reverse vending machines, all of which means increased operational costs for retailers and producers alike. And I'll say that again: for retailers and producers alike. We're talking, again, about another hit on our businesses. 

The British Soft Drinks Association has warned that this decision could increase the cost of some bottles by up to 50p, which on something like a small bottle of water would be a huge proportional increase. Leading Welsh manufacturer Radnor Hills described the Welsh Government's plans as a complete and utter mess. Industry representatives have warned that manufacturers may pass additional costs directly on to consumers or even withdraw products from sale in Wales altogether. Now, I don't know about you, but certainly, if I'm having a beverage, I prefer it out of glass. There's far too much ingestion of plastic now from drinking from plastic bottles. So, there is a consumer choice at stake here.

These are not theoretical concerns, they are warnings from the businesses expected to deliver this scheme, and I've always listened to my businesses in Aberconwy and now Bangor Conwy Môn. Even more worrying is the Welsh Government's failure to appoint a deposit management organisation to run the scheme. With a launch date of October 2027, little more than a year away, there is still no confirmed administrator, IT, infrastructure or real implementation plan, just ideology and an insipid plan that doesn't stand up to any scrutiny and has the potential to damage our businesses. Serious questions do remain unanswered: how will this scheme operate on a day-to-day basis? How much financial support will retailers receive for operating return points? Which small retailers will qualify for exemptions? How will producers prepare their supply chains? Why is the Welsh Government effectively creating a hard border by introducing Wales-only labels? This is the same Government that only yesterday was talking about looking outward, looking out internationally and everything, and yet you want Wales-only labels on bottles. How will local authorities fund glass collections? Businesses simply cannot invest without certainty, yet certainty has been entirely absent throughout this whole process.

The Association of Convenience Stores has made its concerns abundantly clear. It warns that local shops may be forced to purchase more expensive soft-drop reverse vending machines capable of safely handling glass or face the risks associated with manually accepting broken glass. This is a clear health and safety concern. Ed Woodall, chief executive of the Association of Convenience Stores—a cross-party group that I was proud to chair for a full term—warned that, unless an administrator is appointed urgently, Welsh businesses will fall behind the rest of the United Kingdom. He also made another important point: the best chance of success is a deposit-return scheme that is the same throughout the UK. That is what the Welsh Conservatives have always supported from the outset. Sainsbury's, the Co-operative Group and Coca-Cola have all written directly to the First Minister warning that the current policy risks increasing prices, reducing customer choice and creating growing uncertainty for businesses operating in Wales—concerningly, discouraging suppliers trading in Wales altogether. So, why are these warnings from these important businesses, these important industry experts, falling on deaf ears?

These leading industry figures also urge the Welsh Government to appoint Exchange for Change immediately, because they believe it represents the only realistic route to delivering a scheme on time, while ensuring compatibility across all four nations. Yet, despite being the only applicant, Exchange for Change was initially rejected, which is extremely concerning. If this tender is not an attractive proposal to those in the industry, how do you, Cabinet Minister, think you could do a better job of running it? Where would you find the expertise? Where would you create the necessary infrastructure in such a short time frame?

With time running out, the new Welsh Government finds itself struggling to resolve problems of its own making, and the former Welsh Labour Government's own stubbornness. The Welsh Conservatives have consistently warned against creating a separate Welsh system. Businesses trading across the England-Wales border should not be forced to operate different labelling systems, separate supply chains and conflicting regulations. Small Welsh producers should not face unnecessary bureaucracy. Consumers should not face confusion over which containers qualify and which do not. And taxpayers should not face the additional costs of implementing a more complicated system than our neighbours.

The inclusion of glass has already delayed full reuse arrangements involving glass until 2031, recognising that substantial complexities remain. If glass cannot realistically be fully integrated for several more years, why insist on making the initial scheme so unnecessarily difficult now when we want to get on with it? Now we, the Welsh Conservatives, would take a different approach. We would deliver a deposit-return scheme that works from day one. We would align Wales with England, Scotland and Northern Ireland to create one seamless UK-wide system. We would remove glass from the initial phase of the scheme to reduce costs, simplify operations and avoid unnecessary burdens on businesses. We would work in genuine partnership with Welsh manufacturers, convenience stores, hospitality businesses and recycling organisations, rather than imposing these bureaucratic and not-wanted solutions without listening.

Cabinet Minister, surely you can recognise you've backed yourselves into your own corner with this ill-thought-out scheme and unachievable time frame. You said in your own manifesto earlier this year that you would introduce a Welsh deposit-return scheme for plastic and metal drink containers, including glass, when this becomes practically feasible. It isn't practically feasible. You acknowledge the inclusion of glass is problematic, so what has changed?

Why are you hellbent on pressing ahead with this plan? It's going to fail. The cost, the potential for fraud, the cross-border interoperability impact on existing collection systems, the cost to local authorities, the risk of suppliers ceasing trading in Wales and, above all, the cost to the public purse, should this fail, makes the scheme completely unviable and impossible to implement by October 2027. A practical, connected deposit-return scheme would reduce litter, increase recycling and improve environmental outcomes, while supporting Welsh businesses and protecting consumers from unnecessary costs. The inclusion alone of glass threatens to ruin this scheme before it's even implemented.

So, Cabinet Minister, we have so much to be proud of in Wales on our recycling rates. In fact, we've been trailblazers and achieved one of the highest recycling rates in the world. So, it's absolutely critical we get this DRS right. I urge you to support scrapping the inclusion of glass from this scheme, and I urge other Members here to support our stance on this. Diolch.

This is the same Government that only yesterday was talking about looking outward, looking out internationally and everything, and yet you want Wales-only labels on bottles. How will local authorities fund glass collections? Businesses simply cannot invest without certainty, yet certainty has been entirely absent throughout this whole process.

The Association of Convenience Stores has made its concerns abundantly clear. It warns that local shops may be forced to purchase more expensive soft-drop reverse vending machines capable of safely handling glass or face the risks associated with manually accepting broken glass. This is a clear health and safety concern. Ed Woodall, chief executive of the Association of Convenience Stores—a cross-party group that I was proud to chair for a full term—warned that, unless an administrator is appointed urgently, Welsh businesses will fall behind the rest of the United Kingdom. He also made another important point: the best chance of success is a deposit-return scheme that is the same throughout the UK. That is what the Welsh Conservatives have always supported from the outset. Sainsbury's, the Co-operative Group and Coca-Cola have all written directly to the First Minister warning that the current policy risks increasing prices, reducing customer choice and creating growing uncertainty for businesses operating in Wales—concerningly, discouraging suppliers trading in Wales altogether. So, why are these warnings from these important businesses, these important industry experts, falling on deaf ears?

These leading industry figures also urge the Welsh Government to appoint Exchange for Change immediately, because they believe it represents the only realistic route to delivering a scheme on time, while ensuring compatibility across all four nations. Yet, despite being the only applicant, Exchange for Change was initially rejected, which is extremely concerning. If this tender is not an attractive proposal to those in the industry, how do you, Cabinet Minister, think you could do a better job of running it? Where would you find the expertise? Where would you create the necessary infrastructure in such a short time frame?

With time running out, the new Welsh Government finds itself struggling to resolve problems of its own making, and the former Welsh Labour Government's own stubbornness. The Welsh Conservatives have consistently warned against creating a separate Welsh system. Businesses trading across the England-Wales border should not be forced to operate different labelling systems, separate supply chains and conflicting regulations. Small Welsh producers should not face unnecessary bureaucracy. Consumers should not face confusion over which containers qualify and which do not. And taxpayers should not face the additional costs of implementing a more complicated system than our neighbours.

The inclusion of glass has already delayed full reuse arrangements involving glass until 2031, recognising that substantial complexities remain. If glass cannot realistically be fully integrated for several more years, why insist on making the initial scheme so unnecessarily difficult now when we want to get on with it? Now we, the Welsh Conservatives, would take a different approach. We would deliver a deposit-return scheme that works from day one. We would align Wales with England, Scotland and Northern Ireland to create one seamless UK-wide system. We would remove glass from the initial phase of the scheme to reduce costs, simplify operations and avoid unnecessary burdens on businesses. We would work in genuine partnership with Welsh manufacturers, convenience stores, hospitality businesses and recycling organisations, rather than imposing these bureaucratic and not-wanted solutions without listening.

Cabinet Minister, surely you can recognise you've backed yourselves into your own corner with this ill-thought-out scheme and unachievable time frame. You said in your own manifesto earlier this year that you would introduce a Welsh deposit-return scheme for plastic and metal drink containers, including glass, when this becomes practically feasible. It isn't practically feasible. You acknowledge the inclusion of glass is problematic, so what has changed?

Why are you hellbent on pressing ahead with this plan? It's going to fail. The cost, the potential for fraud, the cross-border interoperability impact on existing collection systems, the cost to local authorities, the risk of suppliers ceasing trading in Wales and, above all, the cost to the public purse, should this fail, makes the scheme completely unviable and impossible to implement by October 2027. A practical, connected deposit-return scheme would reduce litter, increase recycling and improve environmental outcomes, while supporting Welsh businesses and protecting consumers from unnecessary costs. The inclusion alone of glass threatens to ruin this scheme before it's even implemented.

So, Cabinet Minister, we have so much to be proud of in Wales on our recycling rates. In fact, we've been trailblazers and achieved one of the highest recycling rates in the world. So, it's absolutely critical we get this DRS right. I urge you to support scrapping the inclusion of glass from this scheme, and I urge other Members here to support our stance on this. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Deputy Presiding Officer. We do indeed have a lot to be proud of here in Wales, don't we? Credit where credit’s due: in terms of recycling, we are absolutely brilliant and world leaders, and kerbside particularly. And if our system to recycle glass ain't broke, why are we fixing it? Reform are not opposed to a deposit-return scheme, but we do argue whether it's actually necessary to do something different for the sake of it. We support practical measures to reduce litter, to improve recycling and protect our environment. We are in sole support of this motion today, and we are opposed to the Welsh Government's decision to create a system separate from the United Kingdom.

This is where the scheme goes from a sensible idea to bureaucratic eco-madness. We are standing on the edge of yet another economic disaster cooked up right here in the Cardiff Bay bubble. The Plaid Cymru minority Government, backed by the leftovers of left Labour's failed policies, is about to push through a scheme so detached from reality that it would be funny if it wasn't dangerous. Now on paper, it sounds lovely, doesn't it? We're going to help the environment. But let's look at the reality. Under their plan, when you buy a drink, you pay a mandatory deposit, and you only get it back if you drag your empty bottles and cans back to the shop. But here's the kicker, the absolute madness that perfectly sums up this establishment in Cardiff Bay: they have insisted on including glass in the Welsh scheme, completely isolating Wales from England, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Think about what that actually means. England, Scotland and Northern Ireland will operate one broadly aligned system, whilst Wales insists on going its own way. This is classic Plaid-Labour politics, making Wales different simply for the sake of being different. People will be buying drinks in Hereford, Chester, Bristol and bringing them back to Wales, whilst businesses will be expected to understand and administer different rules depending on which side of the border they happen to stand on.

The industry itself has warned that this ideological stubbornness opens up a massive risk of cross-border fraud, with the British Soft Drinks Association warning of a potential £300 million fraud risk because our politicians wanted to look virtuous instead of being practical. It is an open invitation for exploitation. And who pays for this? The hard-working people of Wales, who are already battling a brutal cost-of-living crisis. The British Soft Drinks Association has explicitly warned that forcing glass into the scheme could add up to 50p to the cost of a single bottle of drink—50p on one single bottle. Executives from Tesco, Sainsbury's and Coca-Cola have written to the First Minister, warning that this scheme could cause higher prices and a severe reduction in consumer choice. Major brands are already looking at Wales and saying it's not worth the hassle. They are not going to print separate, expensive Wales-only labels just to satisfy Cardiff Bay. Our supermarkets will have emptier shelves and our Welsh families will have emptier wallets. It is terrible news for our economy.

What about our independent retailers? Our shopkeepers are expected to become waste disposal sites. Wine merchants on the border have already said they are deeply concerned about expanding or investing in Wales because the red tape involved in keeping separate Welsh and English stock is completely unaffordable. Cardiff Bay is punishing the very people who keep the Welsh economy alive. And for what? What is the environmental grand prize here? Wales already has, as I've said, world-class kerbside recycling—credit where it's due. Our communities already recycle over 90 per cent of their glass through normal household collections. The system works. But instead of leaving it alone, this Government wants to dismantle a working system. It wants to force elderly residents, busy parents, those who are disabled to load heavy glass into their cars and drive to a supermarket machine just to get their own money back. This does not reduce carbon emissions. It increases them. Think of all those unnecessary and increased car journeys. It's classic Plaid virtue signalling in its most arrogant and absurd way.

Deputy Presiding Officer, the whole roll-out is a complete and utter mess. With less than 15 months until the October 2027 deadline, the Government has not successfully appointed an administrator even to run this scheme. It rejected the only realistic industry applicant because it was blinded by its own dogma. The rest of the UK is using Exchange for Change, but the Plaid Welsh Government rejected it. [Interruption.]

If Wales has no compatible scheme in place when the rest of the UK launches, Welsh consumers could be charged a 20p deposit with no easy way to reclaim it unless they cross the border into England. We will be supporting the Conservative motion today. Diolch.

I welcome the fact that the Conservatives have tabled this debate today and that they agree that Wales needs a deposit-return scheme, and I'm hopeful that that is something that we'll all agree on, actually, this afternoon. What we're talking about when we talk about a deposit-return scheme is a very effective way to tackle the scourge of litter by providing a network of deposit facilities that match up with the increasing prevalence of patterns of on-the-go eating and drinking, which is such a common feature of today's busy society. Janet has talked about litter, and I agree with her. Litter is on our streets, in our parks, in our rivers, on our railway tracks and on our roadside. Litter finds its way into our areas of natural beauty and, sadly, into our seas also. I think we could say that there's cross-party consensus that litter is a blight on all our communities, and it's one of the issues that always comes up in conversations with our constituents.

I'm pleased that, under the previous Welsh Labour Government, we passed legislation to enact a deposit-return scheme and that schemes are also set to be enacted across the rest of the UK. And, as others have mentioned, Wales should be very proud of the fact that we are the second best recycling nation in the world, but litter persists as a problem, and evidence actually suggests that it's getting worse, despite the sterling efforts of local authority street cleaning teams, Keep Wales Tidy and volunteer litter pickers across Wales.

The debate here today is about the form that this deposit-return scheme will take. I've heard the calls, as others have also, from the drinks industry, calling for glass to be excluded from the scheme, but I don't agree that we should follow that path. And the reason for that is because of the increase in prevalence of glass litter. And the figures here are really stark. The occurrence of glass bottles in our litter in Wales has more than doubled over the last four years. By including glass, the scheme will offer a greater environmental benefit, but also, importantly for us on these benches, economic opportunities for green growth, while also exemplifying the approach outlined in the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015.

Now, 'green growth' is a small phrase, but it's really important because what it means is jobs. There's an opportunity here for Wales to lead the rest of the UK when they eventually catch up with us and include glass in their deposit-return schemes, with glass recycling plants in Wales that could lead the way on that, building expertise in an industry that is a sustainable, futureproof green industry. Many other European countries manage to recycle glass through deposit-return schemes without harming the businesses that sell beer bottles and other drinks in glass. Finland is a really good example. It's been offering a deposit-return scheme for glass since 1952. So, I would ask Reform and the Conservatives why they think if other countries can do it, we can't here in Wales. It seems to me that that kind of thinking is talking Wales down, and that's not where I want us to be. The statistics show that deposit-return schemes work to reduce litter and improve our environment, and I want to see the widest possible scheme offering the widest possible benefits and a chance for Wales to create those green jobs for the future. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: I'm grateful to be able to take part in this debate here today. In this Chamber, of course, we've already heard that many of us share the ambition for a deposit-return scheme that builds on Wales's world-leading recycling rates, but I think we must also agree that a good policy must work well in practice, not just look good on paper. And the question is not whether we should improve recycling, but whether creating a separate, more complicated deposit-return scheme than in the rest of the UK is the best way to achieve that.

contributions.text_english:
In answer to previous speakers' challenge back to the Conservatives a moment ago, the fundamental issue here is the divergence away from the rest of the UK and the complexity that creates in the system, increasing the cost, increasing the pressures for businesses and, ultimately, for consumers, who are the ones who will pay the literal cost of this at the end.

As a Member for the Fflint Wrecsam constituency, I see every day how interconnected our communities are here in the UK. People are constantly moving between England and Wales to work, shop and visit family, with businesses trading seamlessly across that border. What they need is that certainty and consistency, not that divergence and additional bureaucracy for bureaucracy's sake. That's why, as Janet Finch-Saunders outlined in her opening, we've consistently supported a fully aligned, cross-nation, four-nation, deposit-return scheme approach.

It's also the position of the Welsh Beer and Pub Association, which has warned that different schemes across the UK will create unnecessary complexity and, ultimately, additional costs. The association has called for a fully aligned, four-nation approach, which would mean excluding glass from the scheme. Glass would create unnecessary complexity and additional costs for producers, retailers—and, again, let's not forget those consumers, who are the ones that would be paying for this through their purchases. Those costs could ultimately lead to higher prices, reduce consumer choice as some brands will reconsider the Welsh market, and greater pressure on smaller Welsh businesses. Again, the previous Labour speaker talked about the opportunities around green growth, but what hasn't been acknowledged is the potential losses because of the higher costs of dealing with this proposed scheme.

The Association of Convenience Stores has raised similar concerns. We'd all share the feeling that local shops are at the heart of communities across Wales, particularly in our rural areas. They'd play a vital role in the success of any deposit-return scheme. Yet, many convenience stores simply do not have the space to accommodate glass returns, and the specialist reverse vending machines required are significantly more expensive. Especially at a time when many independent retailers are already under pressure, this is a very serious concern for them. The inclusion of glass is not simply an environmental question, it's a practical one. We should ask whether it's the right way to achieve our environmental ambitions, without placing unnecessary burdens on retailers, producers, and importantly, again, consumers.

It's already been mentioned in this debate, Deputy Presiding Officer, the question of readiness. With the scheme due to launch in October 2027, a little over a year away, businesses seem to lack the certainty they need. The Association of Convenience Stores, as we've already heard, has urged the Welsh Government to appoint the deposit management organisation as soon as possible so those retailers can invest, adapt their operations and train staff appropriately. Without that certainty, the October 2027 deadline will become increasingly difficult to achieve. I know the Cabinet Minister wants to, perhaps, speak to that point specifically in his response, and I look forward to hearing from him on that.

I also think the Cabinet Minister does get this issue. I know that he sees the problem that businesses are facing at the moment with this and the issues that divergence will create. I ask the Cabinet Minister to reflect on what he, I'm sure, feels in his heart of hearts are the issues this is going to cause, and actually reflect on the costs it's going to cause to businesses. Your Plaid Cymru Government here often talked in their campaign that they wanted the economy at the heart of this new Plaid Cymru Government. So, listen to what businesses are telling you on this scheme at the moment, listen to their concerns and align with the rest of the UK.

So, I ask the Cabinet Minister specifically: will the Welsh Government commit to working with other UK nations to deliver a truly interoperable deposit-return scheme? Will you consider that the inclusion of glass at launch risks increasing costs for Welsh businesses and consumers? Will you acknowledge that? And will you urgently appoint a deposit management organisation so that businesses have the certainty they need to prepare?

Deputy Presiding Officer, I will wrap up by saying that environmental ambition and economic common sense should go hand in hand. We can deliver a successful deposit-return scheme, but only if it is practical, affordable and aligned with the rest of the UK. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

No-one in this Chamber should be indifferent to litter, and we've heard that already. No-one wants plastic bottles and cans on our beaches, in our rivers—I spoke about this when I talked in the rivers debate—in our parks or alongside our roads. Wales can be rightly proud of its environmental record, absolutely, but good intentions do not automatically make good policy, and we should be aware of that today. The test of this deposit-return scheme is not whether recycling matters—of course it does—the real question is whether Ministers are proposing a solution to a genuine problem, or whether they are trying to fix something that is already working remarkably well, particularly with regard to glass.

Llywydd, I have increasingly come to the conclusion that, on glass, the proposal risks moving from sensible recycling into, as Laura Anne Jones mentioned, 'recycling madness'. I actually find it quite amusing that some people speak as if recycling is a modern phenomenon. I grew up in a society where reuse and recycling were simply a part of everyday life. My parents and grandparents belonged to the 'make do and mend' generation. They encouraged the same in me. If something broke, you repaired it; if something could be reused, you reused it. Nothing was thrown away unnecessarily and, as a child, a part of that was actually taking bottles back and getting thruppence, which you'd spend on sweets and things like that, and we did it every week. You took the bottles back to the shop for those few pennies. There was no blue bin in the yard at that stage, so you took things back. Nowadays, there is a blue bin in the yard we can throw glass into.

So, I'm not opposed to the principle of deposit-return schemes, because I grew up with one. I understood the logic behind them. Indeed, I believed in deposit-return schemes long before they actually became fashionable. But life has also taught me something else. A deposit-return scheme only makes sense when it improves upon what already exists, and the Government proposal does not improve upon that. That brings us to the fundamental question before us today: what problem are Ministers actually trying to solve here? Indeed, Wales already, as we've heard, recycles around 92 per cent of household glass through existing collection systems. That's an extraordinary achievement, and we're not underperforming in Wales. We are not the laggards of Europe. We are amongst the best performers anywhere in the world, as other speakers here have said.

So, let's be honest about what is being proposed. This is not a debate about moving from failure to success. It is a debate about imposing significant costs and disruption on Welsh businesses and Welsh consumers in pursuit of what may amount to little more than a marginal improvement. That is the point at which sensible recycling, as I've mentioned, risks becoming recycling madness. Now, don't take my word for it. Yesterday, I met with representatives from the food and drinks industry, and this is what they told me: 'Why should we be expected to work harder, comply with more regulation, absorb more costs and take more risks for no profit at all?' These are not multinational corporations, they're Welsh businesses, Welsh breweries, Welsh food and drink producers, people who employ local workers and invest in local communities.

So, what's the potential answer? Welsh consumers could still pay a 20p deposit on containers sold in Wales, despite there being no practical system through which the money could be reclaimed. Llywydd, that would not feel like an environmental policy to many people; it would feel like a tax on Welsh consumers. So, I ask again: what is the problem that Ministers are actually trying to solve here? If reuse is truly the future, then pilot it, test it, prove it, gather the evidence, but do not place additional burdens on Welsh producers before the evidence exists. Environmental policy must be guided by common sense. There's a difference between environmental responsibility and environmental overreach, there's a difference between solving problems and creating new ones, and there's a difference between sensible recycling and recycling madness. So, we should build on the success we've already got, we should improve on what works, but we should not burden Welsh businesses and Welsh consumers with disproportionate costs in pursuit of marginal gains.

When a country already recycles 92 per cent of its household glass, spending millions to chase the final few percentages—1 per cent, actually, so I believe—is not environmental leadership, it is taking a success story, fixing what is not broken and turning sense into nonsense. That's why I can't support the proposal by the Government, and I actually support the motion. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
There seems to be absolutely no disagreement here in the Siambr that we need to support recycling and a deposit-return scheme. Really, the only thing I am wrestling with is that I seem to agree with the Conservatives in relation to their motion. So, my concern, like has been heard, is the decision to include glass when the rest of the UK is not. And that is why I voted against the DRS scheme when it came around here in the Senedd. There were a few reasons, and one is about listening to businesses. They are the heart and soul, big or small, of our economic system here in Wales. And the other, which is just to respond to the issue of 'Why shouldn't we do it here in Wales when we can see it in other countries?', is that, actually, we have a huge border with another country, a country that I want to continue working with. I don't want us to be independent. So, we need to be looking at how we are going to work with England, who have a huge border with us. Like many, I've spoken to businesses across my constituency, large and small, and the message has been remarkably similar: they support the scheme, they understand why we're doing it, but they're worried about the uncertainty created by a Welsh-only approach to glass.

One conversation that really stuck with me was with a small independent cider producer. This is exactly the sort of business that we want to support. They told me that, even with the proposed four-year transition period, they still don't know how a separate Welsh system for glass will work alongside the rest of the UK. We also spoke to Radnor Hills, which is in my constituency, Wales's largest drinks producer, right on the border with England—literally, they're about five steps away from the English border. Around 95 per cent of their sales are outside Wales. They ask a simple question: does it really make sense to redesign production lines, labels and warehousing for the remaining 5 per cent? The answer clearly, for them, is 'no'. That warning matters because these are the businesses that have to make the scheme work. They need time to trial stores in store reverse vending machines, ensure accessibility, train thousands of colleagues and adapt complex supply chains.

And, as we've heard, we've seen what happens when implementation gets ahead of preparation, in Scotland. We saw that their attempt to launch their own deposit-return scheme was delayed repeatedly before Circularity Scotland collapsed. Wales should learn from that experience, not repeat it. If we do that, Wales can continue to lead on recycling. We need to be listening to our businesses. We need not to be different for the sake of it. We need, in time, potentially, to develop a glass recycling scheme that the rest of the UK has the confidence to adopt. Let's get this right first. Then, let's lead. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Wales has one of the best recycling records in the world. We've heard that several times, and, certainly, I'm proud of what we've done in Monmouthshire, boasting a recycling rate that exceeds the Welsh average. So, this debate is not really about whether we care about recycling—clearly, we all do. The question is whether the Welsh Government is capable of delivering this scheme properly, and, based on what we have seen so far, I have some concerns. But I hope that the Cabinet Minister, being a pragmatic and sensible man who understands the situation, will allay some of our fears.

With just over a year until it is implemented, businesses still do not know how the scheme will run, what exemptions will exist, or how the return points will be funded. Indeed, I was speaking to a retailer here in this building earlier today who was really anxious, not really sure how it was going to work, how they were going to fund it, how she could afford to run the reverse vending machines in her place. So, there are lots of questions unanswered. So, I think being different is not the same as being better. All other UK nations are proceeding with plastic and aluminium, but only Wales, as we know, is insisting on including glass. And as Jane Dodds pointed out just now, we are facing that absurd situation where a glass bottle sold in Hereford operates under one set of rules, yet, across the border in Abergavenny, suddenly the system changes.

Now, businesses trading across the England-Wales border should not have to operate two separate systems simply because the Welsh Government has decided to go its own way. Every additional layer of complexity means additional costs, and those costs ultimately end up being paid by consumers. It is very easy to design a scheme in Cardiff Bay; it is much harder to make it work in a village shop in Monmouthshire, an independent retailer in Cwmbran, or a family-run convenience store serving its local community.

When Coca-Cola, the Co-op and Sainsbury's are all raising concerns, Ministers should pay attention. When Welsh producer Radnor Hills describes the scheme as a complete and utter mess, Ministers should definitely pay attention. Instead, to date, concerns have been brushed aside. So, I ask the Welsh Government: if this scheme is ready, where is the administrator? If implementation is on track, why are key operational decisions still unresolved? If businesses need certainty today, why has the Welsh Government left them waiting until tomorrow? Those are serious questions, and so far Plaid Cymru have not provided convincing answers.

We support a deposit-return scheme, we support higher recycling rates, we support reducing litter and protecting our environment, but environmental ambition must be matched by common sense. A successful scheme must be affordable, workable and aligned with the rest of the United Kingdom. The Welsh Government should abandon this unnecessary disparity, remove glass from the initial roll-out and focus on delivering a scheme that actually works for Welsh consumers, Welsh retailers and Welsh businesses. I encourage all to support our motion.

contributions.text_english:
Now, deposit-return schemes are an internationally proven way to increase recycling, to collect high-quality materials, to support reuse, and that is important, and, of course, to reduce the environmental impact of single-use drinks containers. And for Wales, this offers us an opportunity to build on our recycling success by helping to commence the transition to reuse, drawing from the proven success, as I said, of some of the world's best schemes that are out there. So, getting this scheme right is about ensuring the scheme will work for Wales so that it delivers clear return on investment and brings real benefits to producers, retailers and consumers.

Now, while there may be different views on aspects of the scheme design, I think we can all agree on the shared ambition to introduce a successful deposit-return scheme that works for Wales, whilst being interoperable with the other schemes in the UK. The position on the scope of the scheme has been established, of course, with the Senedd having passed the regulations that are now in law, including the inclusion of glass and the phasing in of reuse. Reopening these fundamental elements would only create further uncertainty and certainly delay the October 2027 launch date being called for by industry, and the benefits that DRS can bring to Wales as well would subsequently be delayed.

Now, I would like to directly address some factually inaccurate claims that I've seen circulating about the costs of this scheme. Let me be clear: figures cited of a DRS in Wales costing £200 million or adding 50p to the price of drinks in glass bottles are not accurate. They relate to industry's upper estimate of the potential cost of fraud in the absence of a scheme in Wales. They don't reflect the scenario that we are working to, and we are clear on the need to bring in a scheme in Wales in parallel with those elsewhere across the UK. In line with the well-being of future generations Act requirements, it's important that we're also taking a long-term view, with DRS playing an important role as an investment in a more sustainable circular economy for Wales longer term.

Businesses have been clear that they need certainty and for the scheme to be delivered in parallel, as I say, with the schemes in the rest of the UK, and the regulations provide a clear framework for industry to prepare, to invest and plan with confidence, and we are committed to working in partnership with industry to deliver the scheme by October 2027. And as has been quoted—as a Government, our manifesto commitment is clear—whilst glass is in scope from the outset, the full requirements in relation to glass need to be implemented pragmatically and when feasible, particularly for SMEs.

So, we're therefore committed, as I say, to working with industry to ensure the practical implementation of the regulations, and we're fully committed to interoperability with schemes across the UK. And with international examples having already demonstrated that variations in scope within a shared single market are entirely deliverable, so interoperability shouldn't be confused with uniformity, and the need to ensure that Wales has a scheme that works for us, as well as the rest of the UK, is perfectly achievable. There are examples; somebody mentioned Finland earlier, and there was reference to a long border in Wales. The Finnish border is about 20 or 30 times longer than the situation we have in Wales. We have US states, of course, that have interoperability that work to very different systems.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr, Ddirprwy Lywydd. I mentioned the US states as well. You know, they are in a similar position. Those aren't the same hard borders that you believe exist everywhere. These schemes can be and will be interoperable. Large tracts of the regulations in Wales actually mirror word for word the regulations in England. It's a journey that we're on. I know exactly where we want to get to, and there's a trajectory that we need to see happening. Wales was given the ability to include glass. We do have the United Kingdom Internal Market Act 2020 because it was seen as an opportunity to see how that could be developed and how that could work, and I'm keen to achieve that, but as I say, working with the industry and working with the people of Wales who have already showed an ambition to go further.

I want to make a point about the appointment of the deposit management organisation; that's where I was. Look, our aim is to take a balanced and pragmatic approach. I was saying that, combining long-term ambition with deliverability, and we currently are working at pace to complete the formal process of appointing a deposit management organisation. There was an assertion made earlier that we had rejected—we hadn't. That had happened under the former Government. We are now picking up from there, and I'm optimistic that we will bring this to a positive conclusion in short order. My focus, and that of my officials, is firmly on making sure that the organisation appointed will be able to deliver a scheme that works in Wales, and it would be inappropriate for me to prejudge the outcome or to comment on any individual applications, because, obviously, the appointment has to be made through a fair, transparent and robust process in line with the regulations. But, as I say, I hope to bring a positive conclusion to that in short order.

As we have learned from international schemes, the appointment of an effective management organisation is a critical milestone in implementation, as once they're appointed, they play a pivotal role, of course, in working with producers, retailers and wider stakeholders to oversee delivery, to provide certainty to the industry and to help ensure that the scheme is launched successfully, as is planned in October 2027. And as has already been mentioned, the scheme in Wales is necessarily different because, of course, our starting point on recycling is very different. We are focused on putting in place a scheme that delivers clear benefits to Wales.

One of my colleagues, Carrie Harper, said in a discussion last week on fair funding that today's underinvestment becomes tomorrow's disadvantage, and the same applies here to the economic opportunities associated with a DRS scheme and the wider circular economy. If Wales is required to wait for others to catch up, then we risk missing out on potential investment, on potential jobs, and the benefits that we're already seeing in our wider economy from our status as one of the best recycling nations in the world. Too often, decisions affecting Wales are made elsewhere by organisations whose priorities might conflict with Welsh interests. Wales should be able, of course, to shape our own future, but we also should be able to capture the value of our own resources and realise the economic benefits of the transition to a circular economy here in Wales, rather than seeing those opportunities accrue elsewhere.

These decisions aren't always the easiest, I accept that, but they are the right ones, and I believe the people of Wales expect us to show that leadership. Diolch yn fawr, Ddirprwy Lywydd. I mentioned the US states as well. You know, they are in a similar position. Those aren't the same hard borders that you believe exist everywhere. These schemes can be and will be interoperable. Large tracts of the regulations in Wales actually mirror word for word the regulations in England. We do have the United Kingdom Internal Market Act 2020 because it was seen as an opportunity to see how that could be developed and how that could work, and I'm keen to achieve that, but as I say, working with the industry and working with the people of Wales who have already showed an ambition to go further.

I want to make a point about the appointment of the deposit management organisation; that's where I was. Look, our aim is to take a balanced and pragmatic approach. I was saying that, combining long-term ambition with deliverability, and we currently are working at pace to complete the formal process of appointing a deposit management organisation. There was an assertion made earlier that we had rejected—we hadn't. That had happened under the former Government. Now, Wales is a leader in this area, Dirprwy Lywydd, and we've already shown that decisive action can deliver real benefits for the environment and for the economy. And by introducing a deposit-return scheme that reflects the unique needs and circumstances of Wales, we can build on our excellent record in recycling, we can reduce litter, we can even increase recycling rates further, but we can also support businesses and communities across Wales and accelerate that transformation into a more circular and low-carbon economy.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. I think anybody watching this debate in this Chamber will be thinking to themselves, 'Look, I recycle already. This issue shouldn't really affect me.' But we all know, all of us here, that it will. It'll affect every single person who buys a drink in a glass bottle; it'll affect shops, supermarkets, convenience stores, online retailers, our high streets; and it will, of course, affect those independent businesses, like breweries, cider makers, and other food and drink manufacturers. But most importantly of all, this is going to affect people's pockets, and it's going to cause them inconvenience.

I want to set out right now that the Welsh Conservatives support recycling. We want to thank the people of Wales for the efforts that they make to recycle. It's something pretty extraordinary that Wales is one of the best recycling nations in the world. That's something we can be really, really proud of. So, we don't object to recycling, but we do object to Wales going its own way on this particular issue because of the confusion, because of the extra cost, because of the unnecessary complexity that this might create.

Our system at the moment isn't broken: 92 per cent of glass containers are currently recycled under the current arrangements, the kerbside arrangements. And this scheme makes recycling more complicated for the consumer and the household. Let's think about this, right? At the moment, you buy some bottles of beer or milkshake, or whatever your preferred beverage might be, or a bottle of HP sauce, and you consume it, and you generally pop that bottle into something that you leave at the end of your drive or outside your front door for the council to collect, very efficiently, in large, usually, very often, electric vehicles that they then take to a local recycling waste transfer centre. Under the new scheme, we're going to expect people to think about, first of all, where they bought that bottle of sauce, where they bought their milkshake—yes, because it's not going to work otherwise on a cross-border basis. You will get this issue of fraud that people have raised. So, they'll have to think, first of all, 'Where did I buy this bottle from? Which shop? Which side of the border do I need to return it to, or can I leave it at the kerbside for collection?' And then, if they bought it from a retailer in England and it's been delivered to Wales, they won't necessarily be able to get the credit for that return if they take it to a local shop. It's absolutely bonkers. And not only that, but they then, after they've worked out where they bought their product, have to jump into their car and drive, causing potential emissions into the environment, all the way to a shop, and that shopkeeper, then, has to find somewhere to store their bottle for another vehicle to come and pick it up, when it could have been picked up by the van passing the end of their road, or the end of their drive, sent by the local council. It's inefficient, it's not necessarily going to be good for the environment.

So, it's bonkers. We don't need it. We need to change the approach. We need a consistent approach across the UK. And I have to say, you must listen to the voice of these retailers, you must listen to these consumers, and you must listen because we have made mistakes before by rushing in. We all remember the 20 mph fiasco in Wales. And I will say this, and it feels like a prophetic moment, you'll see a similar backlash across Wales as a result of introducing this system, Cabinet Minister, if you don't listen. Let these words ring in your ears over the next few months, as you contemplate these matters and decide on the future of a deposit-return scheme.

Diolch. I'm giving a minute to Jayne Bryant and Peredur Griffiths.

I'm grateful for the opportunity to bring forward this short debate on improving access to local economic opportunities in Casnewydd Islwyn. Economic opportunity is not only about whether jobs, courses, schemes or support exist somewhere in the system; it is about whether people can see those opportunities, reach them and use them. People in Casnewydd Islwyn want decent work. They want young people to have a future close to home. They want local businesses to succeed. This depends on the Welsh Government, local government, colleges, employers and community groups working together. But Government has a role in making the system easier to understand and easier to access. This is the argument of this debate.

If a young person cannot see the links between what they study and the work available to them, ambition starts to look like something you have to leave the area to find. We should want people here to see a future in Wales and understand the route to it. If an adult wants to retrain or move into better work, this starting point should not depend on already knowing how the system works. If a local employer wants to expand, take on apprentices or invest in a site, they should know where to go, what support exists and who is responsible. They should not have to chase different parts of the public sector to find out.

Economic development sounds abstract. Its impact is not. A secure job changes a household. A training route gives someone confidence. An apprenticeship changes what a family believes is possible. That is why access to opportunities should be treated as a delivery test. Can people see what is available? Can they reach it? Can they use it?

I want to ask the Welsh Government three things. First, how will you make the local economy offer—skills, training, apprenticeships, employment support and growth sector routes—more visible in constituencies such as Casnewydd Islwyn? Second, how will you strengthen the links between education, skills and local employers so people understand what skills are needed and how to move from one stage to the next? Third, how will you make it easier for local employers to engage with the public sector when they want to grow, invest and create jobs?

This debate is about access. Casnewydd Islwyn has ambition, capable businesses and communities that want to see delivery. The task is to make the route into opportunities clear. This is the spirit in which I bring this debate forward. Thank you.

Coleg Gwent is the largest provider of full-time further education in Wales, with over 18,000 learners, including campuses in Newport and Crosskeys, and the college is a major employer, with over 1,200 staff. The college is seeing record levels of applications for courses, and I think everyone in this Senedd would agree that colleges like Coleg Gwent are vital in preventing young people from being lost to long-term disengagement from education and the labour market. contributions.text_english:
I thank Lyn for giving me time to take part in this debate. We both represent Casnewydd Islwyn, along with Jayne and Natasha and others here in this Chamber. Recently, Lyn and I visited the semiconductor company KLA in Newport. KLA have been a real success story and are about to outgrow the state-of-the-art R&D and manufacturing facility that they have. KLA is part of the CSconnected semiconductor cluster in Casnewydd Islwyn, which supports thousands of jobs directly and many more indirectly through the vast supply chain of local firms. These are well-paid jobs. For example, the average wage at KLA is well over £60,000 a year. KLA conduct outreach work and bring their company and wider industry to the attention of children and young people through visits to schools and work with sports clubs.

What I'd like to know from the Government, and echoing what Lyn has asked, is how this Government can assist companies like KLA to get their message out to our communities and how young people in particular understand that there will be well-paid jobs in a cutting-edge industry and that they are available locally so they don't have to move away from the communities where they grew up. I'd also like to understand, similar to what Jayne was asking, those links with schools, further education and higher education institutions to try and make those pathways for those young people to be able to get into those jobs. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Dirprwy Lywydd, I would like to thank the Member for Casnewydd Islwyn for bringing this debate before us this afternoon, the final debate of this session, on such an important topic. I'm also grateful for the contributions from other Members. This is a valuable debate, not only about the economic future of one constituency, but about the broader role that the south-east of Wales can play in ensuring prosperity for the whole of Wales. This constituency is unique. In one brief journey, you can go from Caerleon, where the Roman legion dwelt, through Newport, the city of the Chartists, and up the valley, through Risca, Newbridge and Abercarn, to Blackwood—communities that built Welsh industry with their own hands.

There are very few constituencies that capture so much of Welsh history in so few miles, and there are few that hold so much of its future: advanced manufacturing, world-leading innovation, public services that are strong, a skilled workforce, digital industries that are growing, and excellent educational institutions. When we talk about economic growth, it's not the scale of the growth that matters alone; the real question is whether that growth actually increases living standards, creates better paid jobs and strengthens communities. That's why this Government has set an ambitious objective for itself and for Wales to halve the productivity gap between Wales and the UK.

'Productivity' isn't a word that warms the cockles of one's heart, perhaps. As far as I know, nobody's written a poem about it—to date, at least. Perhaps at the next Talwrn y Beirdd, we will see that. But its significance is simple and striking. More productive economies pay higher salaries, they attract more investment and create greater opportunities for future generations. If we are serious about the prosperity of the whole of Wales, particularly in those communities that have too often felt that they have been ignored, then we must tackle Welsh productivity. It's not jargon; it's a salary on a Friday, ultimately, it is sustenance for families and for communities.
contributions.text_original:
Ddirprwy Lywydd, hoffwn ddiolch i'r Aelod dros Gasnewydd Islwyn am ddod â'r ddadl hon gerbron, y ddadl olaf yn ystod y sesiwn yma, ac ar bwnc mor bwysig. Dwi'n ddiolchgar hefyd am y cyfraniadau gan Aelodau eraill. Mae hon yn drafodaeth werthfawr, nid yn unig am ddyfodol economaidd un etholaeth, ond am y rôl ehangach y gall de-ddwyrain Cymru ei chwarae wrth sicrhau ffyniant i Gymru gyfan. Mae'r etholaeth yma'n unigryw. Mewn un daith fer, gallwch fynd o Gaerllion, lle cadwai Rhufain ei llengoedd, drwy Gasnewydd, dinas y Siartwyr, ac i fyny'r cwm, drwy Risga, Trecelyn ac Abercarn, i'r Coed-duon—cymunedau a gododd diwydiant Cymru â'u dwylo eu hunain.

Ychydig iawn o etholaethau sy'n dal cymaint o hanes Cymru mewn cyn lleied o filltiroedd, ac ychydig iawn sy'n dal cymaint o'i dyfodol: gweithgynhyrchu uwch, arloesedd sydd yn arwain y byd, gwasanaethau cyhoeddus cryf, gweithwyr medrus, diwydiannau digidol sydd yn tyfu, a sefydliadau addysgol arbennig. Pan fyddwn yn siarad am dwf economaidd, nid maint y twf yw'r unig beth sy'n cyfrif; y cwestiwn go iawn yw a yw'r twf hwnnw yn codi safonau byw, yn creu swyddi gwell eu cyflog ac yn cryfhau cymunedau. Dyna pam mae'r Llywodraeth hon wedi gosod amcan uchelgeisiol iddi hi ei hun ac i Gymru i haneru'r bwlch cynhyrchiant rhwng Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig.

Dydy 'cynhyrchiant' ddim yn air sy'n cynhesu’r galon, efallai. Hyd y gwn i, does neb erioed wedi ysgrifennu cerdd amdano—hyd yma, efallai. Talwrn y Beirdd nesaf, efallai. Rwyf wedi chwilio. Ond mae ei arwyddocâd yn syml ac yn drawiadol, onid yw e? Economïau mwy cynhyrchiol sy'n talu cyflogau uwch, yn denu mwy o fuddsoddiad ac yn creu mwy o gyfleoedd i genedlaethau'r dyfodol. Os ydyn ni o ddifri ynglŷn â ffyniant Cymru gyfan, yn enwedig yn y cymunedau hynny sydd wedi teimlo'n rhy aml eu bod nhw wedi cael eu hanwybyddu, mae'n rhaid i ni fynd i'r afael â chynhyrchiant Cymru. Nid jargon mohono; cyflog dydd Gwener yw e yn y pen draw, cynhaliaeth teuluoedd a chymunedau.

contributions.text_english:
The good news is that Casnewydd Islwyn already holds many of the key ingredients for Wales's economic success. Start with Newport—a city with a habit of arriving early at the future. In 1839, thousands marched down Stow Hill to demand a vote a generation or more before the rest of Britain caught up with them. Newport is early again today. It has become one of Wales's most important economic centres. It is home, as we've heard, to globally significant semiconductor and advanced manufacturing businesses.

The modern world runs on slivers of silicon thinner than a human hair—in our phones, our hospitals, our electric vehicles, in our artificial intelligence—and a remarkable share of that capability globally sits within a few miles of the communities we are discussing this afternoon. Isn't that an exciting thing to say? We were at the heart of an industrial revolution in the past and we are there, right at the centre, at the leading edge today. The growth of the semiconductor cluster in south-east Wales settles an old argument. Wales can compete internationally in high-value, knowledge-intensive industries. Not in theory, but in practice, now. These are precisely the sectors that drive productivity and create the highly skilled, well-paid jobs our communities deserve.

Alongside that industrial strength stands another major asset, the University of South Wales and its Newport campus, of course. A university is not simply a place young people pass through for three years. As an anchor institution, it is part of the economic machinery of the region. Its work in engineering, digital technology, cyber security, business innovation and workforce development helps ensure that local employers can find the skills they need. It provides a vital bridge between research, innovation and commercial opportunity. If Wales is to attract and keep high-value industries, institutions like this one will be central to the mission. The same is true for Coleg Gwent and further education. FE and higher education together, working as a regional version of the team Wales approach, is going to be so central to our economic success.

contributions.text_english:
Newport's strengths reach well beyond manufacturing and higher education. This is now the city where the United Kingdom counts itself and registers its ideas. The Office for National Statistics keeps the nation's numbers—this nation, and the one next door, and the one up north as well. The Intellectual Property Office guards its inventions here. There's something quietly satisfying about a city that for too long has been undercounted, I think, in the national story, being the place that does the counting in so many contexts. More practically, perhaps, these organisations have made Newport a hub for highly skilled employment, drawing talented people into the city and creating room for the private sector to grow around them. Add excellent connectivity through the M4 corridor, the rail network, which we are seeking to build out and build upon, and access to wider regional markets, and Newport has become a nexus, a driver of economic activity, not just for itself, but for the wider region and for the nation as a whole.

The same is true of the Valleys communities that give this constituency its unique character. When Victorian engineers wanted to build the tallest railway viaduct in Britain, where did they choose but Crumlin? Blackwood, Newbridge, Risca and Abercarn carry a proud industrial heritage and a workforce with deep experience in engineering, manufacturing and the skilled trades. These communities built the Welsh economy once, but they're not museum pieces; they have an equally important part to play in building the next Welsh economy too.

Now, our challenge is to make sure that investment reaches every part of Wales and every part of this constituency, and, as you've said, that local people can reach the opportunities being created. That means investing in skills, creating, as the Deputy Minister is now doing, and fashioning a skills system that actually delivers the needs of our employers, but crucially as well allows our young people to achieve their true potential, backing local businesses, improving transport, digital connectivity, enabling people to find quality work close to home.

It also means learning from our own history, and few places teach the lesson better than this constituency. For generations, coal came down these valleys to be burned at Uskmouth and exported out of the port, and too much of the wealth it created went elsewhere. For too long, Wales has hosted energy projects without keeping enough of the value they generate. That must now be reversed. If Welsh land, wind, water and sea bed create wealth, the people of Wales should see more of the value of it. The energy story of Casnewydd Islwyn is already turning. At Uskmouth, the old coal-fired power station is being transformed into one of the largest battery storage hubs in the United Kingdom, storing clean power on the very site that once burned Valleys coal. Beside the steelworks at Llanwern sits one of the largest solar developments in Britain. The uplands above the Sirhowy and Ebbw valleys have the wind, and beneath them, the flooded workings of the old collieries hold warm water that mine water schemes elsewhere are already putting into homes. Even our newest industries point the same way, because a semiconductor cluster is a hungry customer for clean, reliable, affordable power. So, the question for this constituency and for Cymru, for Wales as a whole, is no longer whether the energy transition will happen here, it's who will own it, who will drive it and who will benefit from it. That's the question my work on behalf of the Government on a national energy strategy is designed to answer, and we will explore the levers we can use in Wales to build a strategy that benefits the people of Wales and Casnewydd Islwyn economically and socially, to ensure that we maximise that prize.

The strategy will set an ambitious yet reachable energy target, including targets for local community and Welsh public-owned energy. The Basques have done it. Iberdrola, a Basque company, is one of the biggest giants across Europe now, because they designed their manufacturing system, but also their energy system, around ensuring that the benefit was kept. We can do that in Wales as well.

I think crucial to this, of course—. Private development and private capital, in any economy, will always play a central role, and we want to attract that capital to invest in Wales to enable us to achieve our potential, but we cannot do it alone through private development. That's why developing our own public energy company, as I said, but also co-ordinating across the different parts of Government, across the different organisations—that's going to be essential to ensuring that we achieve the potential in Casnewydd Islwyn and across Wales.

That's why the creation of a new national development agency matters so much. On this very point about the confusing landscape that we have at the moment, we want to actually have a single front door. If I am a business owner or an investor or a founder and I want to know where to go, then we need to simplify and streamline that, because we want to work faster and further with those companies to ensure that we maximise the opportunity, not just for them, but for Wales as a whole. Our vision of a development agency reflects our determination to be more ambitious, more strategic, more proactive. It will work to attract inward investment, but crucially as well develop our own businesses to scale up, to strengthen local and regional economies and deliver the high-value jobs that we need.

Crucially, we understand that there's an important role here for transport; it's not a separate issue from economic growth. That's why we're joined at the hip, myself and the Deputy Minister for Transport, because infrastructure is a key part of how we deliver socially and economically for our nation, and for every part of our nation. The south-east Wales regional transport plan gives us a platform to connect communities in Casnewydd Islwyn and across the wider region. We're building further on that plan. We have an ambitious vision in terms of how transport can contribute to ensuring that we have the potential there.

contributions.text_english:
The south Wales metro is central to that ambition still. It must mean better connectivity between trains, buses and exchanges, and between those and people, as they walk, cycle and scoot, making it easier to reach work, training and education, without having to rely on a car for every journey. For the communities of Casnewydd Islwyn, the test is simple: is the investment increasing real access to opportunities across Casnewydd Islwyn, across the wider region in the Valleys and the Cardiff capital region, and across Wales?

Dirprwy Lywydd, the economic story of Casnewydd Islwyn isn't just a story of potential. It's already a place of significant strengths, higher manufacturing capacity that is internationally recognised, with a digital economy and innovation that is developing, major employers in the public sector, a prominent university and communities with a proud history of skills, resilience and enterprise. Those strengths are firm foundations for the future. As we aim towards halving that productivity gap between Wales and the UK, building the industries of the future and establishing a new development agency to encourage growth and investment, constituencies like Casnewydd Islwyn will be at the heart of our success.

And it's no accident that this constituency carries the name of a poet—Islwyn. There is a theme developing here, isn't there? The poet Islwyn from Ynys-ddu in the Sirhowy valley taught us that all is sacred. He was right. There is nothing ordinary about these communities, or the people, or their future, and the work of building that future is already there.

Our aim is clear. The vision is an exciting one. We can take inspiration from the excellence that we see, as I saw when I visited KLA and saw the future of Wales before my very eyes—young people with the highest level of skills, and a company that has laid down roots in broader clusters in a microcosm of the Wales that we want to create. Thank you.
contributions.text_original:
Mae metro de Cymru yn ganolog i'r uchelgais honno o hyd. Rhaid iddo olygu gwell cysylltiadau rhwng trenau, bysiau a chyfnewidfeydd, a rhwng y rheini a phobl, wrth iddynt gerdded, olwynio a beicio, gan ei gwneud hi'n haws cyrraedd gwaith, hyfforddiant ac addysg, heb orfod dibynnu ar gar ar gyfer pob taith. I gymunedau Casnewydd Islwyn, mae'r prawf yn un syml: a yw'r buddsoddiad yn gwella mynediad go iawn at gyfleoedd ar draws Casnewydd Islwyn, ar draws rhanbarth ehangach y Cymoedd a phrifddinas-ranbarth Caerdydd, ac ar draws Cymru?

Ddirprwy Lywydd, nid stori am botensial yn unig yw stori economaidd Casnewydd Islwyn. Mae eisoes yn lle o gryfderau sylweddol, capasiti gweithgynhyrchu uwch a gydnabyddir yn rhyngwladol, sydd ag economi ddigidol ac arloesedd sy'n tyfu, cyflogwyr mawr yn y sector cyhoeddus, prifysgol flaenllaw a chymunedau â thraddodiad balch o sgiliau, gwydnwch a menter. Mae'r cryfderau hynny'n sylfeini cadarn at y dyfodol. Wrth inni anelu at haneru'r bwlch cynhyrchiant rhwng Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig, adeiladu diwydiannau'r dyfodol a sefydlu asiantaeth ddatblygu newydd i ysgogi buddsoddiad a thwf, bydd etholaethau fel Casnewydd Islwyn yn ganolog i'n llwyddiant ni.

Ac nid damwain yw bod yr etholaeth hon yn cario enw bardd—Islwyn. Mae yna thema yn fan hyn, onid oes? Y bardd Islwyn o Ynys-ddu yng nghwm Sirhywi a ddysgodd inni fod yr oll yn gysegredig. Roedd e'n iawn. Nid oes dim byd cyffredin am y cymunedau hyn, nac am eu pobl, nac am eu dyfodol, ac mae'r gwaith o adeiladu'r dyfodol hwnnw eisoes ar y gweill.

Mae ein nod ni yn glir. Mae'r weledigaeth yn gyffrous. Rŷn ni'n gallu cymryd ysbrydoliaeth o'r rhagoriaeth rŷn ni'n ei weld, fel gwnes i ei weld pan oeddwn i'n mynd o gwmpas KLA a gweld dyfodol Cymru o fy mlaen i—pobl ifanc gyda sgiliau ar eu huchaf, a chwmni sydd wedi rhoi lawr gwreiddiau mewn clystyrau ehangach mewn meicrocosm o Gymru rŷn ni eisiau ei chreu. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much, Minister. And I thank you all again for your contributions this week. That brings today's proceedings to a close.
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr iawn, Weinidog. A diolch i chi eto am eich cyfraniadau yr wythnos yma. Daw hynny â thrafodion heddiw i ben.

Motion NDM9289 Huw Irranca-Davies

To propose that the Senedd, in accordance with Standing Order 16.3, establishes the Llywydd’s Committee to carry out the functions set out in Standing Order 18.B2, and, in accordance with Standing Order 17.3 and 18.B4, elects the following as members of the Llywydd’s Committee:

a) The Deputy Presiding Officer as Chair of the Committee;

b) Sam Rowlands (Chair of the responsible committee under Standing Order 19); and

c) Marc Jones (Plaid Cymru), Stephen Senior (Reform UK), Jayne Bryant (Welsh Labour) and Andrew R.T. Davies (Welsh Conservatives).

tabled_texts.text_english:
Motion NDM9247 Shav Taj [R], Jane Dodds, Paul Rock

Supported by Anna Nicholl, Jayne Bryant, Ken Skates, Kiera Marshall, Lynne Neagle, Mike Hedges, Vikki Howells, Zaynub Akbar

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Notes that too many young people in Wales continue to face barriers to accessing secure, well-paid high-quality employment, contributing to outmigration, economic inactivity and inequality of opportunity.

2. Acknowledges the Welsh Government’s Young Person’s Guarantee, which aims to ensure that all young people aged 16 to 24 can access education, training, employment or self-employment, while recognising that outcomes do not always lead to sustained, good-quality work.

3. Recognises that Wales is an attractive place to live, study and work, with many young people choosing to remain and build their futures here, but notes with concern that Wales continues to lose too many young people to opportunities elsewhere due to gaps in job quality and availability.

4. Acknowledges that many young people experience insecure employment, low pay and limited progression, and that reducing the number of young people not in education, employment or training (NEETs) remains a key ambition, with further progress required.

5. Recognises that some groups of young people, including those with disabilities or long-term health conditions such as brain tumours, young carers, and those from lower-income backgrounds face additional barriers to accessing opportunities, and that access to good-quality employment should not be determined by a postcode lottery.

6. Recognises the importance of creating good quality jobs characterised by fair pay, security, progression and the opportunity presented by economic transitions, including the move to net zero and investment in growth sectors, to expand opportunities for young people.

7. Notes commitments to create jobs for the future and to expand employment and skills opportunities, and stresses the importance of ensuring these translate into accessible, high-quality jobs for young people across all parts of Wales.

8. Notes UK Government action to expand opportunities for young people, including employment and skills programmes and wider investment such as the Warm Homes Plan with significant potential to create jobs in sectors including construction, retrofit and clean energy.

9. Notes with concern regional inequalities in access to employment, skills provision and transport, particularly affecting young people in rural, coastal and post-industrial communities.

10. Calls on the Welsh Government to:

a) strengthen the delivery of the Young Person’s Guarantee to ensure that all young people receive meaningful opportunities leading to secure and well paid employment;

b) set out clear ambitions for reducing the number of young people who are NEET, supported by a focus on progression and long-term outcomes;

c) promote fair work and improve job quality across publicly supported employment and skills programmes;

d) align Welsh employment and skills programmes with wider UK initiatives to maximise opportunities and investment in Wales;

e) outline how it will create and support pathways for young people into growth sectors, including green industries, housing retrofit, advanced manufacturing and the care economy;

f) expand access to high-quality apprenticeships and vocational routes linked to long-term careers;

g) ensure that employment, skills and youth support programmes are inclusive and accessible, including tailored support for those facing additional barriers; and

h) take a strong joined-up approach across economic, housing, education and transport policy to ensure that young people can build a future worth staying for in Wales.
tabled_texts.text_original:
Cynnig NDM9247 Shav Taj [R], Jane Dodds, Paul Rock

Cefnogwyd gan Anna Nicholl, Jayne Bryant, Ken Skates, Kiera Marshall, Lynne Neagle, Mike Hedges, Vikki Howells, Zaynub Akbar

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn nodi bod gormod o bobl ifanc yng Nghymru yn parhau i wynebu rhwystrau i gael mynediad at gyflogaeth ddiogel â chyflog da ac o ansawdd uchel, gan gyfrannu at allfudo, anweithgarwch economaidd ac anghydraddoldeb o ran cyfleoedd.

2. Yn cydnabod Gwarant Pobl Ifanc Llywodraeth Cymru, sy'n anelu at sicrhau bod pob person ifanc rhwng 16 a 24 oed yn gallu cael mynediad at addysg, hyfforddiant, cyflogaeth neu hunangyflogaeth, tra'n cydnabod nad yw canlyniadau bob amser yn arwain at waith parhaus o ansawdd da.

3. Yn cydnabod bod Cymru'n lle deniadol i fyw, astudio a gweithio, gyda llawer o bobl ifanc yn dewis aros ac adeiladu eu dyfodol yma, ond yn nodi gyda phryder bod Cymru'n parhau i golli gormod o bobl ifanc i gyfleoedd mewn mannau eraill oherwydd bylchau o ran argaeledd ac ansawdd swyddi.

4. Yn cydnabod bod llawer o bobl ifanc yn profi cyflogaeth ansicr, cyflog isel a dilyniant cyfyngedig, a bod lleihau nifer y bobl ifanc nad ydynt mewn addysg, cyflogaeth na hyfforddiant (NEETs) yn parhau i fod yn uchelgais allweddol, a bod angen cynnydd pellach.

5. Yn cydnabod bod rhai grwpiau o bobl ifanc, gan gynnwys y rhai ag anableddau neu gyflyrau iechyd hirdymor fel tiwmorau ar yr ymennydd, gofalwyr ifanc, a'r rhai o gefndiroedd incwm is yn wynebu rhwystrau ychwanegol i gael mynediad at gyfleoedd, ac na ddylid penderfynu ar fynediad at gyflogaeth o ansawdd da drwy loteri cod post.

6. Yn cydnabod pwysigrwydd creu swyddi o ansawdd da gyda chyflog teg, diogelwch, dilyniant a chyfle yn sgil trawsnewidiadau economaidd, gan gynnwys symud i sero net a buddsoddi mewn sectorau twf, er mwyn ehangu cyfleoedd i bobl ifanc.

7. Yn nodi'r ymrwymiadau i greu swyddi ar gyfer y dyfodol ac i ehangu cyfleoedd cyflogaeth a sgiliau, ac yn pwysleisio pwysigrwydd sicrhau bod y rhain yn cael eu troi'n swyddi hygyrch o ansawdd uchel i bobl ifanc ar draws pob rhan o Gymru.

8. Yn nodi camau Llywodraeth y DU i ehangu cyfleoedd i bobl ifanc, gan gynnwys rhaglenni cyflogaeth a sgiliau a buddsoddiad ehangach fel y Cynllun Cartrefi Cynnes sydd â photensial sylweddol i greu swyddi mewn sectorau gan gynnwys adeiladu, ôl-osod ac ynni glân.

9. Yn nodi, gyda phryder, anghydraddoldebau rhanbarthol o ran mynediad at gyflogaeth, darpariaeth sgiliau a thrafnidiaeth, sy'n effeithio yn arbennig ar bobl ifanc mewn cymunedau gwledig, arfordirol ac ôl-ddiwydiannol.

10. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i:

a) cryfhau'r broses o gyflawni'r Warant Pobl Ifanc i sicrhau bod pob person ifanc yn cael cyfleoedd ystyrlon sy'n arwain at gyflogaeth ddiogel a chyflog da;

b) nodi uchelgeisiau clir ar gyfer lleihau nifer y bobl ifanc nad ydynt mewn addysg, cyflogaeth na hyfforddiant, gyda ffocws ar ddilyniant a chanlyniadau hirdymor;

c) hyrwyddo gwaith teg a gwella ansawdd swyddi ar draws rhaglenni cyflogaeth a sgiliau a ariennir yn gyhoeddus;

d) alinio rhaglenni cyflogaeth a sgiliau Cymru â mentrau ehangach y DU i wneud y mwyaf o gyfleoedd a buddsoddiad yng Nghymru;

e) amlinellu sut y bydd yn creu a chefnogi llwybrau i bobl ifanc i sectorau twf, gan gynnwys diwydiannau gwyrdd, ôl-osod tai, gweithgynhyrchu uwch a'r economi gofal;

f) ehangu mynediad at brentisiaethau o ansawdd uchel a llwybrau galwedigaethol sy'n gysylltiedig â gyrfaoedd hirdymor;

g) sicrhau bod rhaglenni cyflogaeth, sgiliau a chymorth i bobl ifanc yn gynhwysol ac yn hygyrch, gan gynnwys cymorth wedi'i deilwra i'r rhai sy'n wynebu rhwystrau ychwanegol; a

h) mabwysiadu dull cryf cydgysylltiedig ar draws polisi economaidd, tai, addysg a thrafnidiaeth i sicrhau y gall pobl ifanc adeiladu dyfodol sy'n werth aros amdano yng Nghymru.

Motion NDM9288 Llŷr Powell

Supported by Andrew Griffin, Iain McIntosh, Jason O'Connell, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Notes the continued financial, emotional, and animal welfare impact of bovine TB on Welsh farming families and rural communities.

2. Recognises that bovine TB is a complex disease with multiple routes of transmission, including cattle-to-cattle transmission and infection from wildlife.

3. Regrets that the current approach has failed to command the confidence of many farmers and has not delivered the progress needed towards eradication.

4. Calls on the Welsh Government to:

a) maintain robust biosecurity standards;

b) draw on the advice of the TB Technical Advisory Group in developing a new approach to managing bovine TB;

c) recognise wildlife as a source of infection;

d) enable scientifically validated control methods; and

e) ensure that, in the event that the TB Technical Advisory Group recommends targeted wildlife control, including culling, such recommendations are given full and proper consideration and, where supported by the evidence, form part of the Welsh Government’s approach to bovine TB eradication.

2. Yn cydnabod bod TB buchol yn glefyd cymhleth gyda sawl llwybr trosglwyddo, gan gynnwys trosglwyddo o wartheg i wartheg a haint o fywyd gwyllt.

3. Yn gresynu bod y dull presennol wedi methu ag ennyn hyder llawer o ffermwyr ac nad yw wedi cyflawni'r cynnydd sydd ei angen tuag at ddileu.

4. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i:

a) cynnal safonau bioddiogelwch cadarn;

b) manteisio ar gyngor y Grŵp Cynghori Technegol TB wrth ddatblygu dull newydd o reoli TB buchol;

c) cydnabod bywyd gwyllt fel ffynhonnell haint;

Motion NDM9287 Paul Davies

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Congratulates the people of Wales on achieving one of the highest recycling rates in the world.

2. Supports the establishment of a deposit-return scheme in Wales to further improve recycling rates.

3. Believes that unnecessary regulatory divergence from England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and the inclusion of glass in the Welsh Government's current proposed deposit-return scheme will;

a) increase costs for Welsh producers, retailers and consumers;

b) present a risk of significant cross-border fraud; and

c) risk undermining public goodwill.

4. Calls on the Welsh Government to scrap current plans to include glass in the Welsh deposit-return scheme, to ensure alignment between Wales and the rest of the UK.
tabled_texts.text_original:

a) cynyddu costau i gynhyrchwyr, manwerthwyr a defnyddwyr yng Nghymru;

b) cyflwyno risg o dwyll trawsffiniol sylweddol; ac

c) peri risg o danseilio ewyllys da y cyhoedd.

4. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i ddileu'r cynlluniau presennol i gynnwys gwydr yng nghynllun dychwelyd ernes Cymru, er mwyn sicrhau aliniad rhwng Cymru a gweddill y DU.
